Name: causal_correlational_discrepancy
Title: When the Model Disagrees with the Textbook: Using Interpretable-Feature Interventions to Discover Causal Structure-Property Rules That Contradict Correlational Biophysics
Short Hypothesis: Sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models encode two kinds of structure-property associations: those that merely reflect correlations in training data, and those the model uses causally during generation. By comparing a feature's CORRELATIONAL association with a property (how often it co-occurs) against its CAUSAL effect (what happens to the generated object's property when it is clamped), we can systematically surface DISCREPANT features - cases where a well-established correlational structure-property rule is not causally exploited by the model, or where the model imposes a causal rule with no known correlational basis. We hypothesize such discrepancies are numerous, are enriched for genuine confounded/non-causal rules (validated against physics-based counterfactuals), and constitute a hypothesis-generation engine for design rules.
Related Work: Two lines are relevant. (1) SAE feature discovery in scientific models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; the chemistry-LM SAE 2025; motif-gated domain-recognition causal patching 2025) shows features correlate with biological/chemical concepts and that some are causally necessary for a PREDICTION task. (2) Latent causal discovery (PerturbLearn attribute graphs 2022; active causal ML for molecules 2024) extracts causal graphs among attributes. Crucially, all discovery work either (a) reports concept-CORRELATION of features, or (b) verifies causal effect for a single prediction task, but NO work systematically contrasts a feature's correlational property-association with its causal generative effect to identify DISCREPANCIES, nor uses those discrepancies as a filter for finding structure-property rules that are correlational-but-not-causal (spurious) versus causal-but-uncatalogued (novel). Prior steering work treats agreement between correlation and causation as assumed; we treat their DISAGREEMENT as the scientific signal. This reframes interpretability from cataloguing what the model represents to auditing which structure-property rules are actually causal, and validates the model's verdicts against independent physics-based counterfactuals - a genuinely new use of feature interventions.
Abstract: Structure-property rules are the backbone of protein and molecular design, yet many textbook rules are correlational and may not reflect causal mechanism. Scientific foundation models have absorbed enormous data and, through sparse autoencoders (SAEs), expose interpretable features linked to structural and property concepts. We propose to use these features to audit structure-property rules by contrasting two quantities per feature: its CORRELATIONAL association with a property (co-occurrence across natural objects) and its CAUSAL effect on the property of GENERATED objects when the feature is clamped during generation. Features where these disagree - strong correlation but weak causal effect, or strong causal effect with weak correlation - are 'discrepant' and, we hypothesize, are enriched for spurious (confounded) or previously-uncatalogued causal design rules. We instantiate this on ESM-2 protein LMs and a SMILES chemistry LM with residual-stream SAEs, using cheap in-silico property evaluators (DSSP/ESMFold, GRAVY, thermostability probes; RDKit logP/QED/functional groups). For each discrepant feature we generate a design-rule hypothesis and independently adjudicate it with a physics-based counterfactual test - constructing matched object pairs that differ only in the feature-linked structural element and measuring the property with an oracle NOT derived from the model - to determine whether the model's causal verdict or the correlational rule is correct. We report the rate and structure of discrepancies, their enrichment for known confounded rules (positive controls), and case studies of candidate novel causal rules. The framework turns feature interventions into an auditable engine for discovering and stress-testing scientific design rules.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream (intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer) and a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M) with a residual-stream SAE; a Matryoshka SAE variant for robustness. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens from 500k-object subsets, 3 SAE seeds. Feature bank: interpretable, property-linked features selected by concept-correlation/probe AUROC on held-out natural objects. Cheap evaluators on FINISHED objects: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy (light fine-tuned head), motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules - RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, specific functional groups (SMARTS). For each (feature, property) pair: a Correlational score (point-biserial / mutual information between feature activation and property over a large natural sample) and a Causal score (property change per unit steer at low strength within the validity budget, from a strength sweep with unsteered and norm-matched random-direction controls; validity gated by pseudo-perplexity/pLDDT or RDKit-validity). Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - discrepant features are numerous): Tests whether plotting correlational vs causal score surfaces many features where the two disagree. Decisive metric: discrepancy rate = fraction of (feature, property) pairs whose residual from the correlation=causation diagonal exceeds a noise band set by test-retest variance of the two scores. Convincing result: discrepancy rate >= 15% of pairs, with the off-diagonal mass beyond the noise band. Decision band: discrepancy rate in [5%, 15%] -> discrepancies exist but are uncommon. Negative result (< 5%, i.e. correlation tracks causation) is itself valuable, establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules, and refutes H1. Quadrants reported: (A) high-corr/low-causal (candidate spurious), (B) low-corr/high-causal (candidate uncatalogued causal), (C) concordant; rates broken out per domain, model size, SAE variant.

Experiment 2 (H2 - discrepancies are enriched for genuinely non-causal rules): Tests whether the discrepancy map recovers KNOWN spurious rules and whether an independent physics oracle sides with the model over the textbook on adjudicated cases. Decisive metric: agreement rate between the model's causal verdict and an independent physics adjudication on a sample of discrepant pairs. Convincing result: the discrepancy filter attains precision >= 0.7 on a labeled set (known-spurious rules landing in quadrant A, known-causal in C), AND physics adjudication agrees with the model's causal verdict on >= 70% of adjudicated discrepancies. Decision band: precision or agreement in [0.5, 0.7] -> partial validation. Negative result (near-chance precision/agreement) refutes H2. Data: a literature-curated set of known confounded and known causal structure-property associations (as many as the literature supports across both domains); matched counterfactual object pairs differing only in the feature-linked structural element (single-motif insert/delete or point substitutions for proteins; minimal SMARTS edits with matched scaffolds for molecules); the adjudication oracle (FoldX/Rosetta or MD-lite for proteins; RDKit/empirical logP or docking for molecules) is deliberately independent of the generative model's training signal; matching quality reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 - discrepancies are a design-rule engine): Tests whether quadrant-B causal-but-low-correlation features act as design levers where correlational-only rules fail. Decisive metric: success rate of producing the target property in NEW designs when steering the causal (quadrant-B) feature versus applying the correlational-only rule. Convincing result: causal-rule success >= 2x correlational-only success and >= 0.10 absolute. Decision band: causal-rule success between 1.2x and 2x correlational-only -> a real but modest advantage. Negative result (causal rules no better than correlational) refutes H3. Auto-generated human-readable candidate rules (feature label + measured causal effect) are the deliverable; robustness reported across two model sizes, two SAE architectures, and both domains.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico correlational and causal scores and physics adjudicators are all imperfect proxies; the strongest claim is triangulated agreement/disagreement among independent in-silico signals, not wet-lab truth. To reduce circularity, the adjudication oracle is deliberately chosen to be independent of the generative model's training signal. 2) Discrepancies could arise from SAE artifacts (entangled features, poor reconstruction) rather than genuine causal/correlational structure; we mitigate with multiple SAE architectures, probe verification, and random-direction controls. 3) Constructing clean matched counterfactuals is hard, especially for proteins where a single edit can change many things; we restrict to minimal, well-controlled edits and report matching quality. 4) The positive-control set of known spurious/causal rules may be small, limiting enrichment power; we include as many labeled rules as the literature supports across both domains. 5) A feature's causal score depends on layer/strength; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test layer sensitivity. 6) If discrepancies turn out to be rare (correlation almost always matches causation), that is itself a valuable, publishable result establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules.

The novel claim is turning the mismatch between correlational property association and causal generative effect into a discovery engine for spurious vs uncatalogued design rules, then validating against an independent physics oracle. That combination is meaningfully new if executed as framed.

Name: shared_concept_causal_bridge
Title: One Knob, Two Worlds: Do Proteins and Molecules Share Causally-Steerable Physicochemical Concepts in a Unified Sparse Autoencoder?
Short Hypothesis: Abstract physicochemical concepts (hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity) are represented by SHARED interpretable directions in a jointly-trained cross-modality sparse autoencoder spanning a protein language model and a small-molecule language model, and—critically—steering a single shared feature causally and simultaneously controls the corresponding property in BOTH modalities' generations. We further hypothesize that shared features are MORE causally steerable and validity-preserving than modality-private features encoding the same concept, because they capture a modality-invariant physical abstraction.
Related Work: Two threads meet here but have never been combined for causal generative control across scientific object types. (1) Cross-model/cross-modal SAEs—USAE (2025), SPARC (2025), and group-sparse multimodal SAEs (2026)—learn shared concept dictionaries across vision/language models, and 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) shows scientific foundation models across string/graph/3D/protein modalities are representationally aligned and collapse when extrapolating. (2) Single-modality scientific SAE steering—InterPLM (2024), the chemistry-LM SAE (2025), Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B (2025), CB-pLM (2024)—discovers and steers interpretable features WITHIN one model of one object type. Crucially: (a) all cross-modal SAE work is descriptive/retrieval-focused and never tests CAUSAL steering of generation; (b) all scientific steering work is confined to a single object type and never asks whether a concept has a single unified causal handle across proteins AND molecules. MolBind (2024) and protein-GDM alignment (2024) align modalities via contrastive learning but do not extract interpretable, individually-steerable, causally-validated shared features. We are the first to (i) train a unified SAE bridging a protein LM and a molecule LM, (ii) identify shared physicochemical concept features, and (iii) test whether ONE shared feature causally steers the SAME property in both modalities' generations—turning cross-modal interpretability from a similarity metric into a shared design lever.
Abstract: Physicochemical concepts such as hydrophobicity, charge, aromaticity, and molecular size govern the behavior of both proteins and small molecules, yet generative models for each object type are studied in isolation and steered by modality-specific machinery. We ask a simple, elegant question: is there a single interpretable 'knob' that controls the same property across worlds? Building on recent cross-model sparse autoencoders (USAE, SPARC), we train a unified sparse autoencoder that jointly reconstructs the residual-stream activations of a protein language model (ESM-2) and a small-molecule SMILES language model, encouraging shared latent dimensions via a cross-reconstruction objective and global sparsity. We identify SHARED features—dimensions that activate coherently in both modalities on a common physicochemical concept—versus modality-private features. Our central test is causal: we clamp a single shared feature and measure whether it simultaneously and monotonically shifts the corresponding property in BOTH protein generations (GRAVY hydrophobicity, net charge, aromatic content via DSSP/biopython) and molecule generations (RDKit logP, formal charge, aromatic-ring count), while preserving validity (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity for proteins; RDKit-validity, synthetic-accessibility for molecules). We compare shared-feature steering against steering matched modality-private features and against difference-of-means directions per modality. We hypothesize shared features act as unified, physically-grounded causal handles that steer more reliably and with a better control-validity frontier than private ones. Success would establish modality-invariant interpretable design levers, letting a single validated concept-knob transfer intent across proteins and molecules and offering mechanistic evidence for a shared physical abstraction in scientific foundation models.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Protein side (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M; molecule side (frozen): a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M, ChEMBL-trained). Residual-stream activations at a mid layer (intrinsic-dimension-elbow) collected for a large protein corpus (500k-sequence UniRef sample) and molecule corpus (500k-molecule ChEMBL/ZINC sample); no paired protein-molecule data is used - alignment is concept-level via the shared objective. Unified SAE: a joint TopK / global-TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) ingesting either modality with modality-specific encoder/decoder heads and a cross-reconstruction term (USAE/SPARC-style); a group-sparse variant for robustness; 3 SAE seeds. Baseline: two independent per-modality SAEs. Per-modality reconstruction fidelity and the fraction of cross-modally active latents (dictionary sharing rate) reported. Concept set {hydrophobicity, net charge, aromaticity, molecular size, polarity} with per-modality evaluators: proteins - GRAVY, net charge at pH7, aromatic-residue fraction, molecular weight, a polarity index (Biopython); molecules - RDKit logP, formal/partial charge, aromatic-ring count, MW, TPSA. Generation: masked infilling / activation-conditioned decoding (proteins), activation-steered autoregressive decoding (SMILES); 5 seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 - shared concept directions exist in the joint SAE): Tests whether physicochemical concepts are carried by single latents active and property-correlated in BOTH modalities. Decisive metric: number of the 5 concepts admitting a SHARED feature (high concept-correlation in both modalities), and the sharing rate versus the independent-SAE baseline (which cannot produce shared indices). Convincing result: >= 3 of 5 concepts admit a shared feature, at a sharing rate above a co-labeling chance control. Decision band: 2 of 5 concepts shared -> partial sharing; report which concepts resist sharing. Negative result (<= 1 of 5, i.e. a split dictionary) refutes H1 but informatively bounds cross-modal abstraction. Matched modality-PRIVATE features (equally high correlation in only one modality) are recorded for Experiment 3.

Experiment 2 (H2 - one knob controls the property in both worlds): Tests whether clamping a single shared feature causally moves the property in each modality's generations. Decisive metric: bidirectional causal success rate = fraction of shared features that produce a significant, correctly-signed property shift in BOTH modalities. Convincing result: bidirectional causal success >= 0.5, exceeding random-direction and unrelated-feature controls, with consistent sign/monotonicity across modalities and validity retained (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity; RDKit-validity, SA). Decision band: bidirectional success in [0.3, 0.5] -> some shared knobs work; report which concepts. Negative result (< 0.3 or not above controls) means co-labeling did not imply a unified causal handle, refuting H2. Data: each shared feature clamped over a swept range, 200 objects per modality per setting.

Experiment 3 (H3 - shared features beat modality-private ones): Tests whether shared features are more steerable and validity-preserving than private features encoding the same concept. Decisive metric: control-validity Pareto frontier area for (i) the shared feature, (ii) the best matched modality-private feature, (iii) per-modality difference-of-means directions, per concept. Convincing result: the shared feature's frontier area is >= the best private feature's at equal validity for a majority of concepts, with better cross-modal steering-sign consistency. Decision band: shared within +-10% of private frontier area -> parity, not superiority; report as "shared no worse." Negative result (shared clearly below private) refutes H3. Supporting analyses: cross-modal steerability Spearman rho (does a shared feature's steerability in one modality predict the other; genuine handle if rho >= 0.5) and a transfer demo (validate a concept knob once on the cheap molecule model, apply the same shared feature to steer protein generation, report fraction of native effect recovered). Robustness across two protein sizes, two SAE variants, and layer choices.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico property evaluators and validity metrics (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, cross-modal controllability, not experimental viability. 2) The joint SAE may learn a 'split dictionary' where most features stay modality-private (the known failure mode from multimodal SAE work); we mitigate with global-TopK and group-sparse objectives and report sharing rate honestly—a low sharing rate is itself an informative result about the limits of cross-modal abstraction. 3) A feature co-labeled as shared could reflect coincidental concept-correlation rather than a unified causal handle; the bidirectional causal test and cross-modal steerability-prediction analysis are designed to distinguish these. 4) Proteins and molecules have very different tokenizations and activation statistics, which may make joint reconstruction hard; we control by comparing to independent per-modality SAEs and reporting per-modality reconstruction fidelity. 5) Steering the molecule LM and masked/infilling protein generation are different decoding regimes; we standardize property measurement on finished objects and use random-direction controls to ensure comparability. 6) Layer/strength choices could confound sharing and steerability; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test multiple layers and SAE variants.

Name: steerability_emergence_pretraining
Title: When Does a Design Lever Get Forged? Tracing the Pretraining Emergence of Causal Feature Steerability in Protein Language Models
Short Hypothesis: In protein language models, the causal STEERABILITY of an interpretable feature (its ability to control the corresponding property in generation) emerges LATER in pretraining than its DECODABILITY (linear readout of the concept), and the emergence time of both is gated by the training-data frequency of the underlying biological concept: rare-but-valid concepts become decodable long before—or without ever—becoming steerable. This decodability-steerability lag is a training-time phenomenon that explains the widely-reported 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly and predicts which design levers a given checkpoint can and cannot provide.
Related Work: Two literatures converge but have never met. (1) Feature-emergence-during-pretraining work is entirely in TEXT LLMs: 'Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training' (2025) and 'Crosscoding Through Time' (2025) use crosscoders to track feature formation; 'The Birth of Knowledge' (2025) maps categorical feature emergence across time/space/scale; and most relevantly 'How Does Controllability Emerge in LMs During Pretraining' (2025) shows linear STEERABILITY of text concepts emerges at intermediate stages and varies by concept, linked to linear separability. None studies scientific generative models, none ties emergence to training-DATA-FREQUENCY of the concept, and none contrasts decodability vs causal steerability trajectories for GENERATED scientific objects. (2) Protein-SAE work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; automated neuron labelling 2025; motif-gated causal patching 2025) is entirely inference-time on a FINAL checkpoint, and reports the 'decodable-but-inert' anomaly as a static puzzle. Data-scaling/bias work (Scaling and Data Saturation in pLMs 2025; pLMs biased by unequal sequence sampling 2024; Compute-Optimal pLMs 2024) shows data frequency shapes likelihoods but never connects it to feature steerability. We are the first to (i) trace decodability AND causal steerability trajectories across pretraining in a scientific generative model, (ii) test data-frequency as the gating variable via curated rare/common concepts and yearly-snapshot corpora, and (iii) reframe the decodable-but-inert anomaly as a training-time developmental lag with a predictive rule for checkpoint-conditional controllability. This uses Formation Tracing—a genuinely different mechanism strategy from prior inference-time steering studies.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design assumes that if a concept is decodable from a protein language model it can be used as a design lever—yet multiple studies report 'decodable-but-inert' features that read out a concept perfectly but fail to steer generation. We propose that this anomaly is a developmental one: during pretraining, the causal STEERABILITY of a feature emerges strictly later than its DECODABILITY, and both are gated by how frequently the underlying biological concept appears in the training data. We test this by pretraining small ESM-style masked protein LMs (3.5M–35M params, tractable for an academic lab) and saving frequent checkpoints, complemented by publicly available yearly UniRef-snapshot pLMs. At each checkpoint we train a sparse autoencoder and, for a curated bank of concepts spanning a wide data-frequency range (common folds/motifs to rare families and rare property combinations), we measure two trajectories: decodability (probe AUROC of the concept feature) and steerability (causal property change per unit steer in generation, verified by DSSP/ESMFold/HMMER). We hypothesize (i) a consistent decodability-then-steerability ordering with a measurable lag, (ii) that concept training-frequency predicts both onset times, and (iii) that some rare concepts remain decodable-but-inert at convergence—explaining the static anomaly. We further test whether an emergent 'steerability onset' at one scale predicts onset at another, and whether upsampling a rare concept in a controlled retraining accelerates its steerability onset. Results would recast steerability as a trainable, data-dependent developmental property and yield a predictive, frequency-based rule for which design levers a checkpoint can provide.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by all experiments below). Models: masked protein LMs in the ESM-2 family at three scales, 3.5M, 8M, and 35M parameters, trained from scratch by us on a fixed 20M-sequence random subset of UniRef50 (UniRef50 has ~60M clusters; we use 20M to keep one 8M/35M run inside a single-GPU-week on one A100-40GB). All weights trainable during pretraining; frozen at each checkpoint for probing/steering. Key hyperparameters: masking rate 15%, batch 2048 sequences, max length 256, LR 4e-4 cosine with 2k warmup, AdamW, ~1.0e10 tokens total; we save 18 checkpoints log-spaced in tokens (10^7 ... 10^10). Three pretraining seeds {0,1,2} per scale for the 3.5M and 8M models, one seed for 35M (budget). Independent data-frequency axis: the four public yearly UniRef-snapshot ESM checkpoints where released. SAE: one TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 8192, trained 100M activations, seed 0) per checkpoint on the mid-layer residual stream (layer at 60% depth), reconstruction FVU reported; a raw-activation linear probe is the SAE-independent control. Concept bank: 40 concepts with hard automated evaluators and exact training-corpus frequency (counted in our 20M subset): 12 common (alpha-helix and beta-sheet fraction via DSSP on ESMFold, GRAVY hydrophobicity, molecular weight, zinc-finger and catalytic-triad motifs via HMMER/PROSITE), 28 deliberately rare (rare Pfam families with 50-500 corpus hits, uncommon motifs, and rare property combinations such as high-beta + high-hydrophilicity). DECODABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = held-out probe AUROC of the best SAE feature (and raw-activation probe) on 2,000 natural sequences. STEERABILITY(concept, checkpoint) = property change per unit steering norm during masked-infilling generation at the largest strength that keeps validity (pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x of unsteered and ESMFold pLDDT >= 0.6*baseline), verified by the concept's own evaluator over 500 generations, with random-direction and unrelated-feature controls subtracted.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Decodability emerges before steerability: the lag). Tests that within a concept, DECODABILITY crosses its detection threshold at an earlier training-token count than STEERABILITY. Data: the 40-concept bank above, evaluated at all 18 checkpoints x 3 scales. Systems compared, per concept: decodability trajectory vs steerability trajectory across checkpoints. Define onset = first checkpoint at which a trajectory crosses a fixed threshold (decodability AUROC >= 0.75; steerability >= 2x the matched random-direction control effect and property change >= 0.5 SD of the natural-sequence property distribution). Decisive metric: paired difference lag = log10(steerability-onset tokens) - log10(decodability-onset tokens), aggregated over concepts (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Hedges g). Convincing positive: median lag >= 0.3 log10-tokens (i.e. steerability onset at >= 2x the tokens of decodability onset) with signed-rank p < 0.01 in >= 2 of 3 scales. Decision band: median lag in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is INDECISIVE given our 18-checkpoint spacing (a lag below the ~0.13-log10 gap between adjacent checkpoints cannot be resolved); we then densify checkpoints x2 around detected onsets before concluding. Negative result: median lag <= 0 (steerability never later than decodability) refutes the developmental-lag account and is reported as such, constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly to non-temporal causes.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Concept training-frequency gates both onsets, correlational). Tests that higher corpus frequency predicts earlier decodability-onset and steerability-onset, and that steerability-onset is the more frequency-sensitive of the two. Data: the same onsets from Experiment 1 paired with each concept's exact corpus frequency (range 50 to ~2M hits across the 40 concepts). Model: mixed-effects regression of log10(onset tokens) on log10(frequency), random intercept per scale and per concept-family. Decisive metric: standardized slope beta_freq for each onset type and the contrast beta_steer - beta_decode. Convincing positive: beta_freq significantly negative for both (higher frequency -> earlier onset) with steerability strictly more sensitive, |beta_steer| - |beta_decode| >= 0.15 (95% bootstrap CI excludes 0). Decision band: contrast in [0.05, 0.15) means frequency gates onset but the differential sensitivity is UNRESOLVED at n=40 concepts; we report the main frequency effect and flag the contrast as underpowered rather than claim asymmetric gating. Negative: beta_freq CI includes 0 means frequency does not gate onset, sending the causal test (Experiment 3) to adjudicate whether a confound (concept complexity, conservation) drives the null.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Upsampling a rare concept causally accelerates its steerability-onset). Tests the gating claim causally by manipulating frequency alone. Data/model: retrain the 3.5M model (cheapest, 3 seeds) with 6 chosen rare concepts upsampled 10x versus a matched control run, total tokens held fixed at 1.0e10 so only relative frequency changes. Systems compared: upsampled vs control run, on the 6 treated concepts and 6 untreated rare controls. Decisive metric: shift in steerability-onset (log10 tokens) for treated concepts, upsampled minus control, paired across seeds. Convincing positive: treated concepts advance their steerability-onset by >= 0.3 log10-tokens (95% CI excludes 0) while untreated controls shift by < 0.1 log10-tokens. Decision band: treated advance in [0.1, 0.3) log10-tokens is a WEAK causal effect; we report it as directional support insufficient to claim frequency is the dominant lever. Negative: treated shift indistinguishable from control (< 0.1) means frequency is not the causal gate, overriding any correlational signal from Experiment 2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- The lag explains decodable-but-inert and predicts a checkpoint's usable levers). Tests that concepts which are decodable-but-inert at convergence are exactly those whose steerability-onset never crosses threshold, and that this is predictable cheaply. Data: convergence checkpoint (10^10 tokens) of all three scales; plus cross-scale onset ordering from all checkpoints. Systems compared: (a) per concept at convergence, decodable-but-inert label (AUROC >= 0.75 AND steerability < threshold) vs the frequency-plus-small-model-onset predictor; (b) steerability-onset ordering at 3.5M vs at 35M. Decisive metrics: (a) fraction of the 40 concepts that are decodable-but-inert at convergence, and AUROC of predicting that label from {log-frequency, 3.5M steerability-onset}; (b) Spearman rho between 3.5M and 35M steerability-onset ranks. Convincing positive: a non-trivial inert fraction (point estimate reported with Wilson CI) with predictor AUROC >= 0.80, and cross-scale rho >= 0.6 (p < 0.01), giving a cheap-model rule for which levers a target checkpoint provides. Decision band: predictor AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) or rho in [0.4, 0.6) means the anomaly is real but only partially predictable; we ship the predictor with its measured error rather than as a guarantee. Negative: inert fraction ~0 (no concept is decodable-but-inert at convergence) means the static anomaly does not reproduce in our models and the explanatory claim is withdrawn; AUROC ~0.5 or rho ~0 means the lag is not predictable and offers no practical lever-forecasting rule.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Small self-trained pLMs may underperform large models, so absolute steerability could be weak; we mitigate by focusing on RELATIVE trajectories/orderings and by cross-checking with public yearly-snapshot pLMs. 2) SAE quality varies across checkpoints and could confound emergence timing; we control with a fixed SAE architecture/hyperparameters per checkpoint, report reconstruction fidelity, and cross-validate decodability with an SAE-independent raw-activation probe. 3) In-silico evaluators (ESMFold, DSSP, HMMER) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal, training-time controllability, not experimental viability. 4) Frequency-onset correlations could reflect confounds (concept complexity, sequence conservation) rather than raw frequency; the controlled upsampling retraining (experiment 7) is designed to isolate frequency causally. 5) Checkpoint spacing may miss sharp emergence transitions; we use log-spaced checkpoints and can densify around detected transitions. 6) If decodability and steerability emerge simultaneously (no lag), that is still an informative, publishable result refuting the developmental-lag account and constraining explanations of the decodable-but-inert anomaly. 7) Retraining runs add compute cost but are limited to the smallest models to stay within an academic budget.

Name: hazard_entanglement_asymmetry
Title: Easy to Arm, Hard to Disarm: An Entanglement Asymmetry Between Hazardous and Benign Design Features in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: In molecular and protein generative models, interpretable features exhibit a dual-use entanglement asymmetry: hazardous structural properties (toxicophores, known toxin/venom motifs, reactive groups) can be AMPLIFIED cheaply by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features, yet cannot be SUPPRESSED without disproportionate collateral loss of valid, benign design capability. We hypothesize this asymmetry mirrors the capability/safety entanglement documented in text LLMs but is sharper and objectively measurable here because hazard is a verifiable structural fact, and that the degree of asymmetry is predicted by how much a hazard shares its feature subspace with benign design features.
Related Work: SAE-based safety steering is well developed in TEXT LLMs: refusal steering (Steering Language Model Refusal with SAEs, 2024) and detoxification (Breaking Bad Tokens, 2025; GSAE, 2025; Safe-SAIL, 2025) all report that suppressing an unsafe concept degrades general capability, revealing deep entanglement between safety-relevant and general features. Separately, scientific-model interpretability (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; pathology-FM SAEs 2024; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) discovers and steers interpretable features toward single BENIGN target properties, treating hazard only implicitly. The 'Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design' review (2025) notes models undersample rare regions but does not study hazard controllability. No prior work (a) transfers the safety/capability-entanglement phenomenon into SCIENTIFIC generative models where hazard is a structurally-verifiable fact (RDKit SMARTS toxicophores, HMMER toxin motifs) rather than fuzzy text behavior, (b) tests a DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY between cheap hazard amplification and costly hazard suppression, or (c) ties that asymmetry to feature-subspace overlap between hazard and benign design. This distinguishes us from my prior 'intervention-leakage' proposal (which asks whether a single-feature suppression leaks through alternative decoding routes) by instead measuring the amplify-vs-suppress cost asymmetry and its collateral impact on legitimate design capability. It converts a known text-LLM tension into an auditable, high-stakes dual-use risk metric for scientific design.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design promises controllable scientific generation, but control is dual-use: the same interpretable knobs that add a desired property may also arm a model to produce hazardous objects, and safety measures that suppress hazard may cripple legitimate design. Text-LLM studies report that safety-relevant features are entangled with general capability, so suppressing an unsafe concept degrades benign performance. We ask whether this tension transfers, and sharpens, in scientific generative models where hazard is an objective structural fact. We define hazardous properties with hard, non-model evaluators (toxicophore/PAINS/reactive-group SMARTS in molecules; known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs in proteins) and benign design properties with cheap oracles (logP, QED, secondary-structure content, foldability). Training sparse autoencoders on a SMILES chemical language model and ESM-2, we test a central phenomenon: an entanglement asymmetry in which hazard is cheaply AMPLIFIED by steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features (a small steering budget, high validity), but cannot be SUPPRESSED below baseline without a disproportionate drop in valid benign-design capability. We quantify an Asymmetry Index = (cost to suppress) / (cost to amplify) and a Collateral Ratio = benign-design loss per unit hazard removed, comparing single-feature, subspace, and difference-of-means interventions and controlling for the known pitfall that SAE-reconstructed steering vectors are unreliable. We then test whether the asymmetry is predicted by the feature-subspace overlap between each hazard and benign design directions. Results would establish a measurable, mechanistically-grounded dual-use risk profile for scientific generative models and a practical audit for whether hazard can be safely disarmed without breaking legitimate design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (a public ~90M-parameter checkpoint pretrained on ChEMBL/ZINC) and ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters. All base weights frozen; only SAEs are trained. SAEs: TopK (k=32) and Matryoshka variants, dictionary 16384, trained on 200M residual-stream activations at a mid layer (60% depth), seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. HAZARD properties, hard non-model evaluators: molecules -- toxicophore/PAINS SMARTS and reactive/electrophilic-group and structural-alert counts via RDKit (10 alert classes); proteins -- known toxin/venom/cytolytic motifs via HMMER against curated toxin HMMs plus regex (8 motif classes). BENIGN design properties, cheap oracles: molecules -- logP band, QED, ring/scaffold target, synthetic accessibility (SA); proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, a fold/foldability target. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA<=6 for molecules; ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline for proteins. Steering budget = L2 norm of the added intervention vector, in units of the mean residual-stream norm at the site (so "0.5" = half the typical activation norm); all costs reported in these normalized budget units. Every intervention uses SAE decoder directions and difference-of-means directions DIRECTLY (never SAE re-encodings of steering vectors, the documented OOD/sign pitfall), with a norm-matched random-direction control. 18 hazard/motif classes total across domains; 500 generations per condition.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Benign knobs cheaply amplify hazard). Tests that steering ostensibly-benign, property-labeled features raises hazard occurrence in finished objects at a small budget. Data/systems: for each of the 18 hazard classes, feature bank of benign property-labeled features (identified by probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) vs the hazard's own features; compare amplification via benign features, via hazard features, and via norm-matched random directions. Decisive metric: AMPLIFICATION COST = minimal budget to raise hazard occurrence in valid finished objects from baseline to 50%. Convincing positive: median amplification cost via benign features <= 0.5 budget units (and clearly below the random-direction control, which should need >> 1.0 or never reach 50% within validity). Decision band: cost in (0.5, 1.0] units is MODERATE -- hazard is amplifiable but not "cheap"; we report it as amplifiable-with-effort, not cheap arming. Negative: benign features cannot reach 50% hazard within the validity budget at any tested strength (up to 2.0) means benign knobs do not arm the model, refuting H1 for that class.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Suppression is disproportionately costly: the asymmetry). Tests that driving hazard below baseline costs far more, and damages benign design, than amplification does. Data/systems: same hazard classes; interventions are single-feature, k-dim subspace (SVD of correlated hazard features), and difference-of-means, each compared to a norm-matched random-direction suppression control. Decisive metric (primary): ASYMMETRY INDEX = suppression cost / amplification cost, where suppression cost = minimal budget to drive baseline hazard occurrence below 5% while holding validity. Secondary: COLLATERAL RATIO = benign-design success loss per unit hazard-occurrence removed, benign-design success = hitting a battery of legitimate targets (logP/QED/scaffold; secondary-structure/fold). Convincing positive: median Asymmetry Index >= 3 (suppression >= 3x costlier than amplification) with Collateral Ratio significantly above the random-direction control (95% bootstrap CI over classes excludes 1x). Decision band: Asymmetry Index in [1.5, 3) is a WEAK asymmetry -- reported as present but modest; in [0.67, 1.5) hazard is essentially as cheap to suppress as to amplify (symmetric). Negative: Asymmetry Index <= 0.67 or Collateral Ratio at/below the random control means hazard can be cleanly disarmed -- a valuable positive safety result reported as refuting the asymmetry.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Objectively measurable and sharper than the text-LLM analogue). Tests that the entanglement here is quantifiable against a structural ground truth and at least as sharp as the reported text-LLM capability/safety degradation. Data/systems: the Collateral Ratio and validity/diversity curves from Experiment 2, benchmarked against a norm-matched random-direction suppression (the text-LLM-style "generic capability degradation" reference) within the same pipeline. Decisive metric: gap between hazard-suppression Collateral Ratio and the random-direction Collateral Ratio at equal hazard removal, plus the fraction of hazard classes whose ratio exceeds the random reference. Convincing positive: hazard-specific suppression shows Collateral Ratio strictly above random in >= 70% of classes (structured, not generic, entanglement) with every quantity computed from hard structural evaluators (0% reliance on a learned hazard model). Decision band: 50-70% of classes above random is PARTIAL -- entanglement is structured for some hazards only; we enumerate which. Negative: <= 50% (hazard suppression no worse than a random norm-matched edit) means the collateral is generic capability loss, not hazard-specific entanglement, and the "sharper here" claim is withdrawn.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- Subspace overlap predicts the asymmetry). Tests that a hazard's feature-subspace overlap with benign design directions predicts its Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio, and that orthogonalized suppression lowers collateral. Data/model: for each hazard class compute subspace overlap with benign directions (mean principal-angle cosine / effective shared rank) from the SAE dictionary; regress Asymmetry Index and Collateral Ratio on overlap (Spearman, bootstrap CI over 18 classes). Mitigation arm: subspace suppression projecting out only the hazard-specific complement (orthogonalized against benign directions) vs plain suppression at equal hazard removal. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between overlap and Asymmetry Index; and Collateral-Ratio reduction from orthogonalized vs plain suppression. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.6 (p<0.05) AND orthogonalized suppression cuts Collateral Ratio by >= 30% at matched hazard removal. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.6) means overlap is one factor among several -- reported as partial predictor; orthogonalized-suppression gain in [10%, 30%) is a modest mitigation. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means overlap does not predict the asymmetry (the mechanism claim fails, though the phenomenon from Experiments 1-2 may still stand), and no orthogonalization benefit means the collateral is irreducible in feature space.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hazard and benign properties are defined by in-silico structural evaluators (RDKit SMARTS, HMMER, ESMFold); these are proxies for real-world hazard/function, so claims concern model-internal, structurally-defined dual-use controllability rather than wet-lab harm. We deliberately study only structural-alert-level hazards with unambiguous detectors and avoid synthesizable-threat detail. 2) The asymmetry could depend on steering budget definition; we sweep budgets and report full amplify/suppress curves rather than single points. 3) SAE quality/layer choice may confound which features 'encode' hazard vs benign; we control with multiple SAE variants, probe verification, difference-of-means directions, and random-direction controls, and we avoid the SAE-reconstructed-steering-vector pitfall documented in the literature. 4) Subspace-overlap predictor may be underpowered with few hazard classes; we include many toxicophore/motif classes across both domains. 5) If no asymmetry is found (hazard is as easy to suppress as amplify, with low collateral), that is a valuable, publishable positive safety result establishing that scientific generative models can be cleanly disarmed. 6) We will responsibly report aggregate metrics and mitigations (orthogonalized suppression), not recipes for producing specific hazardous objects.

The core finding/mechanism could be novel if it holds, though it is an extension of an established entanglement theme rather than a wholly new theory.

Name: steering_fails_on_memorized_designs
Title: You Can't Steer a Memory: Interpretable-Feature Control Silently Fails on Memorized Scientific Designs
Short Hypothesis: Scientific generative models occupy a hybrid regime that memorizes some outputs (near-verbatim training retrievals) and generalizes others. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering, the dominant paradigm for controllable design, CAUSALLY FAILS on memorized generations while succeeding on generalized ones—because memorized objects sit at contractive attractors whose internal representations are 'spiky' and resist perturbation. Consequently, a cheap, intervention-free representation-spikiness score predicts, before any steering, whether a given generation is controllable, and steering evaluated only on aggregate averages hides a large, systematically uncontrollable memorized subpopulation.
Related Work: Two lines converge here for the first time. (1) Memorization geometry: 'Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space' (2025) proves memorized samples yield spiky representations and are NOT steerable while generalized samples are steerable in representation space; 'Overparameterized autoencoders implement associative memory' (2018/2020) shows memorized examples are contractive attractors. (2) Scientific-model controllability: InterPLM (2024), ProtSAE (2025), and chemistry-LM SAE steering demonstrate interpretable features steer protein/molecule generation, but ALWAYS report AGGREGATE property gains and never partition outputs by memorization status. Meanwhile 'Transformer Learning in Sequence-Based Drug Design Depends on Compound Memorization' (2026) and protein-LM data-leakage studies (2024/2025) show scientific generative models are heavily memorization-driven, yet treat this as a benchmark-inflation problem, not a controllability problem. No prior work (a) tests whether the memorized-not-steerable geometry transfers to SCIENTIFIC generative models where memorization is objectively measurable via sequence identity to the training set, (b) shows interpretable-feature steering causally fails on the memorized subpopulation, or (c) validates a pre-flight spikiness score that predicts per-generation controllability. This distinguishes the proposal from all my prior steering-focused ideas (which assumed the target is steerable) and from the memorization literature (which ignores controllable design).
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering has become the standard tool for controllable design of proteins and molecules, and it is universally evaluated by average property gains across many generations. We ask whether that average conceals a systematic failure mode. Recent geometry work shows generative models occupy a hybrid regime—memorizing some outputs as contractive attractors with 'spiky' internal representations while generalizing others—and that memorized samples resist representation-space steering. Scientific generative models are known to be heavily memorization-driven, and, uniquely, memorization here is objectively measurable: a generation is memorized if it is near-identical to a training sequence. We hypothesize that interpretable-feature steering causally fails on memorized generations while succeeding on generalized ones, so aggregate steering metrics hide a large uncontrollable subpopulation. Using ESM-style protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we label each generation as memorized or generalized via sequence/structure identity to the (known) training corpus, then measure per-generation steerability of feature interventions against cheap property oracles. We test three claims: (1) steering property-gain and validity are far lower on memorized than generalized generations at matched steering budget; (2) an intervention-free representation-spikiness score (activation standard deviation / SAE-feature concentration) predicts per-generation steerability before any intervention, enabling a pre-flight controllability filter; and (3) nudging generation away from memorized attractors (light noise/temperature or a 'de-spiking' repulsion from the nearest training neighbor) restores steerability, at a measurable novelty cost. Results would reveal a hidden, safety- and IP-relevant blind spot in controllable scientific design and provide a cheap test for when steering can be trusted.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators with KNOWN training corpora so memorization is objectively measurable: a self-trained ESM-style masked protein LM at 8M and 35M parameters on a defined 10M-sequence UniRef50 subset (one seed each; base weights frozen after training), plus a public ProtGPT2 checkpoint with a documented training set; and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M) trained by us on a defined ChEMBL/ZINC subset. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Cheap property oracles: proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); molecules -- RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional-group SMARTS. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). Feature bank: property-linked SAE features (probe AUROC>=0.8 on 2,000 held-out natural objects) plus difference-of-means directions as a non-SAE baseline. Steering budget in normalized activation-norm units (as in the norm of the added vector / mean site activation norm). Per-generation STEERABILITY = target-property change per unit budget within the validity gate, with norm-matched random-direction control subtracted.

Experiment 1 (H4/H1 -- Memorization labels split a large corpus, and the aggregate average hides the split). Tests that a substantial memorized subpopulation exists and that reporting only the mean steering gain conceals it. Data: 20,000 unsteered generations per model. Labels: MEMORIZED if nearest-training-example identity is high -- proteins: sequence identity >= 90% (mmseqs2/BLAST), optionally TM-score corroborated; molecules: Morgan-fingerprint Tanimoto >= 0.9 or exact canonical-SMILES match; GENERALIZED if nearest identity is low (proteins <= 50%, molecules Tanimoto <= 0.4). Decisive metric: memorized fraction per model (Wilson CI) and its dependence on model size and sampling temperature; plus the bimodality (dip test) of the aggregate per-generation steering-gain distribution. Convincing positive: memorized fraction >= 10% for at least one model AND the aggregate steering-gain distribution is significantly bimodal (dip test p<0.01) once split by label. Decision band: memorized fraction in [3%, 10%) means the blind spot exists but is small -- reported as a minority subpopulation; dip-test p in [0.01, 0.05) is suggestive-only bimodality. Negative: memorized fraction < 3% across all models means no meaningful memorized subpopulation exists here and the aggregate-blind-spot claim (H4) does not apply to these models.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Steering fails on memorized, succeeds on generalized). Tests the core causal-status contrast at matched budget. Data/systems: memorized vs generalized generations matched on baseline property value and sequence length (to remove confounds); apply feature steering and difference-of-means steering at a swept budget {0.1...1.0}; norm-matched random-direction control. Decisive metric (primary): steerability GAP = generalized minus memorized per-generation steerability, mixed-effects model with memorization status as key factor (effect size, 95% CI), plus the control-validity frontier area per subpopulation. Convincing positive: generalized steerability exceeds memorized by >= 0.5 SD of the per-generation steerability distribution (CI excludes 0) with the same ordering in >= 3 of the 4 models. Decision band: gap in [0.2, 0.5) SD is a REAL but modest effect -- reported as partial, not "causal failure"; the aggregate frontier likely still usable on memorized. Negative: gap <= 0.2 SD (memorized as steerable as generalized) is a clean negative result that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to these sequence models, and H1 is withdrawn.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Intervention-free spikiness predicts controllability pre-steer). Tests that a cheap representation-spikiness score forecasts per-generation steerability before any intervention, and does so at least as well as the expensive memorization label. Data: all labeled generations from Experiment 1. Spikiness scores at the intervention site: activation SD across dimensions; SAE-feature concentration (top-feature mass fraction / feature-vector entropy); local contractivity proxy (representation change under small input perturbation). Systems: spikiness vs concept-correlation vs the (expensive) memorization label as predictors of the measured steerability from Experiment 2. Decisive metric: Spearman rho and R^2 of spikiness-vs-steerability, and precision@k for selecting the top-k most steerable generations. Convincing positive: rho >= 0.5 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) AND precision@100 >= 0.8 AND spikiness matches or beats the memorization-label predictor -- a usable intervention-free pre-flight filter with quantified compute saved. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5) or precision@100 in [0.6, 0.8) means spikiness is a weak screen -- reported with its measured error, not as a reliable gate. Negative: rho <= 0.3 means spikiness does not predict steerability and the pre-flight-filter claim fails, even if the H1/H2 phenomenon holds.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- The attractor mechanism: leaving the memorized attractor restores steerability). Tests causally that spikiness/contractive-attractor geometry, not merely the memorization label, is what blocks steering. Data/systems: on memorized generations, apply three de-attractor interventions before steering -- (a) mild temperature/nucleus widening, (b) initial-token/masked-position perturbation, (c) explicit "de-spiking" repulsion from the SAE-representation of the nearest training neighbor -- each vs an untreated memorized control. Decisive metric: steerability gain (post minus pre de-attractor) on memorized generations, paired; reported jointly with the NOVELTY cost (drop in nearest-training-neighbor identity) and validity cost. Convincing positive: de-spiking raises memorized steerability to within 0.2 SD of the generalized baseline (recovering >= 60% of the Experiment-2 gap) at a novelty cost that keeps outputs below the memorized identity threshold. Decision band: gap recovery in [30%, 60%) is partial causal support -- the attractor account is one contributor; recovery achievable only at novelty cost that itself de-memorizes the object is reported as confounded (spikiness and memorization not separable here). Negative: no steerability gain from any de-attractor intervention means the contractive-attractor mechanism is not what blocks steering, so H2 is unsupported even if H1 holds descriptively.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Requires knowing the training corpus to label memorization; we mitigate by self-training small models on defined subsets and using public checkpoints with documented training sets, and by using high-similarity thresholds that give conservative memorized labels. 2) In-silico oracles/validity (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal controllability and design reliability, not experimental viability. 3) Lower steerability on memorized generations could be confounded by their baseline property values or length; we control via matched-pair comparison and mixed-effects modeling. 4) Spikiness might merely correlate with memorization rather than causing low steerability; experiment 6 (de-spiking restores steerability) is the causal test that disentangles this. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could affect both spikiness and steerability; we control with multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 6) If steering turns out equally effective on memorized generations, that is still a valuable, publishable negative result establishing that the diffusion-model memorized-not-steerable geometry does NOT transfer to scientific sequence models—constraining theories of memorization geometry across modalities. 7) The de-spiking restoration trades novelty for controllability; we quantify this frontier rather than assume a free lunch.

Name: infeasibility_frustration_features
Title: Confidently Impossible: Do Interpretable Features Reveal When a Scientific Generative Model Is Fulfilling a Physically Infeasible Design Spec?
Short Hypothesis: When a multi-constraint design specification is physically INFEASIBLE (no valid object can satisfy it), scientific generative models do not refuse or signal failure—they confidently emit a plausible-looking object that silently violates one constraint. We hypothesize the model internally 'knows' the spec is over-constrained: a compact set of interpretable sparse-autoencoder 'frustration' features fire during generation specifically under infeasible specs, and monitoring them yields an early, calibrated infeasibility alarm that output-side confidence signals (perplexity, constraint-satisfaction probability) fail to provide.
Related Work: SAE interpretability of scientific models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; the antibody SAE 2025; ProtoMech 2026; Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B 2025) discovers and steers features toward SATISFIABLE single or multiple properties, always assuming a valid target exists, and evaluates whether the property appears. Hallucination-detection SAE work in text/vision LMs (SSL 2025; 'Do I Know This Entity?' 2024) shows features can flag when a model lacks knowledge, but concerns fuzzy factuality, not physically-verifiable constraint infeasibility. Constraint-based design/steering (compositional steering; conditioned generation) presumes feasibility and reports average satisfaction, never asking what happens when the requested constraint set is CONTRADICTORY. No prior work (a) constructs graded feasible-vs-infeasible design specs for proteins/molecules with objective, physics-based feasibility labels, (b) shows models silently and confidently violate constraints under infeasible specs, or (c) identifies interpretable 'frustration/infeasibility' features that fire selectively and act as a calibrated early alarm. This reframes interpretability from a controllability tool into an epistemic-honesty/safety instrument for design, distinct from all my prior steering-focused proposals and from hallucination work in non-scientific domains.
Abstract: Scientific generative models are increasingly asked to satisfy multiple design constraints at once, but some constraint combinations are physically infeasible—no valid protein or molecule can meet them (e.g., a compact fold with extreme surface-exposed hydrophobicity, or a small-molecule target combining mutually exclusive substructure and property demands). We surface a safety-relevant behavioral phenomenon: rather than refusing, models confidently generate a fluent, plausible-looking object that silently violates one constraint, and standard output-side confidence signals do not flag this. We then ask whether the model internally represents the infeasibility. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we build graded feasibility ladders—specs ranging from clearly satisfiable to provably infeasible—with objective feasibility labels derived from physics/enumeration (e.g., co-occurrence bounds in natural data, RDKit/SMARTS satisfiability, structure-property incompatibility checks). We first quantify the silent-violation behavior and show output-side confidence is uninformative. We then search for interpretable 'frustration' features whose activation during constrained generation rises specifically as specs become infeasible, verify they are causal (ablation/steering shifts violation behavior and constraint-conflict resolution) and interpretable (they fire on the conflicting structural elements), and evaluate them as an early, calibrated infeasibility alarm versus perplexity and constraint-probability baselines. Success would give practitioners a cheap internal test that a requested design is impossible—before expensive synthesis or validation—and recast interpretable features as an epistemic-honesty instrument for scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters and a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~90M), all base weights frozen. SAEs: TopK (k=32, dictionary 16384) and Matryoshka on the mid-layer (60% depth) residual stream, trained on 200M activations, seeds {0,1}, FVU reported. Constraint evaluators (hard, non-model): proteins -- secondary-structure fraction (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, net charge, molecular weight, motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules -- RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, functional-group SMARTS, molecular weight. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT>=0.6 + pseudo-perplexity within 1.5x baseline (proteins); RDKit-validity + SA<=6 (molecules). FEASIBILITY LADDERS: for 24 constraint pairs/triples per domain, a graded ladder from clearly feasible to provably infeasible, with objective labels triangulated from three model-independent signals -- (a) empirical joint co-occurrence support over a 1M-object natural corpus (spec outside joint support = candidate-infeasible), (b) SMARTS/structure-incompatibility rules (mutually exclusive substructures; protein structure-property conflicts such as >80% beta-sheet AND high solvent-exposed hydrophobicity), (c) an oracle-search control -- a genetic optimizer over sequences/molecules with a large fixed budget whose persistent failure corroborates infeasibility. Core claims are restricted to ladder rungs where all three signals agree; label confidence reported per rung. Constraint steering uses property-feature and difference-of-means directions.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Silent violation under infeasible specs, and output-side confidence is blind). Tests that as feasibility drops, models emit valid, fluent objects that violate exactly one constraint rather than refusing, and that output-side confidence does not track feasibility. Data/systems: steer generation toward each spec across all ladder rungs, 500 generations per rung; compare behavior across the feasibility gradient. Decisive metric (primary): SILENT-VIOLATION RATE = fraction of infeasible-spec generations that remain valid/fluent but violate exactly one constraint (vs refusing/degenerating), with the sacrificed-constraint identity tallied for systematicity; secondary: discrimination (AUROC) of output-side confidence (pseudo-perplexity, generation likelihood, a constraint-satisfaction probe) for true feasibility. Convincing positive: silent-violation rate >= 60% on all-signals-agree infeasible rungs AND output-side-confidence AUROC in [0.45, 0.60] (near chance). Decision band: silent-violation rate in [40%, 60%) means the behavior is common but not dominant -- reported as such; output-side AUROC in (0.60, 0.70] means output confidence is a weak-but-nonzero feasibility signal, tempering the "fail to provide" claim. Negative: silent-violation rate < 40% (models often refuse/degenerate) OR output-side AUROC > 0.70 (output confidence already flags infeasibility) refutes H1's framing and removes the need for an internal alarm.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A compact set of frustration features fires specifically under infeasible specs). Tests that identifiable SAE features discriminate infeasible-vs-feasible specs while controlling for constraint identity (so they detect CONFLICT, not one property). Data: SAE features scored at multiple generation-progress fractions across the ladders. Systems: per-feature discrimination of infeasible-vs-feasible, computed WITHIN matched constraint identity, vs the best single-property feature as a baseline. Decisive metric: AUROC (and mutual information) of the top-m frustration-feature set for infeasibility, and its sparsity (how many features reach AUROC>=0.75). Convincing positive: a compact set (<= 20 features) reaches AUROC >= 0.80 for infeasibility while single-property-feature baselines stay <= 0.65 -- i.e. the signal is conflict-specific, not property-specific. Decision band: top-set AUROC in [0.65, 0.80) means partial internal representation of infeasibility -- reported as weak evidence; if the property-feature baseline also reaches >= 0.65 the features may track a single property, flagged as unresolved. Negative: no feature set exceeds AUROC 0.65 for infeasibility beyond the property baseline means the model does not compactly represent over-constraint, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Frustration features are causal for conflict resolution). Tests that intervening on the frustration features changes the model's silent-violation behavior specifically. Data/systems: ablate the frustration-feature set and, separately, amplify it, vs random-direction and matched-single-property-feature controls, on infeasible-spec generations. Decisive metric: change in which constraint is sacrificed (shift rate) and in violation magnitude under ablation; change toward hedging/lower-confidence completions under amplification. Convincing positive: ablation shifts the sacrificed-constraint distribution or violation magnitude by an effect size >= 0.5 SD beyond both controls (CI excludes controls), establishing specificity. Decision band: effect in [0.2, 0.5) SD above controls is weak causal support -- reported as correlational-leaning. Negative: intervention indistinguishable from controls means the features are not causal for conflict resolution and the "model knows" claim reduces to a decodable correlate, reported honestly.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Early, calibrated infeasibility alarm beating output-side signals). Tests that the frustration-feature score read off mid-generation gives an earlier and better-calibrated infeasibility alarm than output-side confidence and a black-box probe. Data/systems: deploy the frustration-feature score at generation-progress fractions {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}; baselines -- partial perplexity/likelihood, a constraint-satisfaction probe on the partial object, and a black-box raw-activation probe. Decisive metric (primary): forecast AUROC for infeasibility vs generation progress, plus calibration ECE; secondary: earliest progress fraction at which AUROC>=0.80 (earliest-reliable-detection) and precision@k for flagging infeasible specs. Convincing positive: the frustration-feature alarm reaches AUROC>=0.80 by 50% progress with ECE<=0.10, beating output-side baselines by >= 0.10 AUROC at that progress point, with quantified compute saved by aborting infeasible requests before full generation + ESMFold/validation. Decision band: alarm AUROC in [0.70, 0.80) at 50% progress, or advantage over the black-box probe in [0.03, 0.10) AUROC, means the internal alarm works but its edge over cheaper signals is marginal -- reported with the interpretability/localization payoff as the differentiator. Negative: the frustration-feature alarm does not beat partial-perplexity/constraint-probe baselines (advantage <= 0.03 AUROC) means output-side signals suffice and the internal-alarm contribution collapses to interpretation only.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Feasibility labels are the crux and are imperfect: empirical co-occurrence support, SMARTS/structure incompatibility rules, and oracle-search failure are all in-silico proxies for true physical infeasibility. We mitigate by triangulating three independent signals and restricting core claims to specs where all three agree, and by reporting label-confidence-stratified results. 2) 'Infeasible' vs merely 'rare/hard' is a continuum; the oracle-search control and graded ladder are designed to separate genuinely impossible from hard-but-possible, but boundary cases will be noisy—reported explicitly. 3) In-silico validity/property evaluators (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal epistemic signals, not experimental viability. 4) Frustration features might merely track the individual conflicting properties rather than their conflict; the constraint-identity control in feature selection and the causal conflict-resolution test are designed to rule this out. 5) The internal alarm may not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; even so, interpretability (localizing the conflict), calibration, and early detection are the contribution and are reported honestly. 6) If models turn out to reliably signal infeasibility via output confidence, that is still a valuable positive result about epistemic honesty in scientific generative models. 7) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled via multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) define graded feasible-vs-infeasible design specs with objective labels; (2) show scientific LMs silently and confidently violate impossible specs; (3) discover interpretable SAE 'frustration' features that fire on infeasibility rather than property presence; (4) use them as an early alarm. Relative to SAE hallucination and steering work, the delta is substantial: the problem shifts from 'does the model know a fact/property?' to 'does it recognize impossibility under hard physical constraints?'. The closest prior family is hallucination/uncertainty detection plus SAE steering on satisfiable scientific properties; the actual novelty is the feasibility framing and the hard-label setting, not SAEs themselves.
