Name: steering_hysteresis
Title: No Undo Button: Does Interpretable-Feature Steering Leave Irreversible Scars on Scientific Generative Designs?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering in scientific generative models is not a reversible knob: applying a feature-steer and then removing it (or applying the exact opposite steer) does NOT return generation to its original design, but leaves a persistent 'scar'—residual, often unintended, changes in the finished object. We hypothesize this steering hysteresis is systematic (not noise), larger for iterative/autoregressive generation where an early perturbation contaminates all downstream decisions, and predicted by how early the steer is applied and by feature-decoder overlap—making the naive 'undo/adjust' workflow that designers assume silently unreliable.
Related Work: Nearly all interpretability-guided design work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs through SAEs' 2025; the chemistry/diffusion SAE steering papers; DLM-Scope 2026; 'Enabling Precise Topic Alignment via SAEs' 2025) treats a steering vector as a reversible, dial-like control: add it to move a property, implicitly assuming you can dial it back or fine-tune around it. Steering is always evaluated in the FORWARD direction (does the target property appear?) and never for REVERSIBILITY. Separately, a physics/biology literature on representation irreversibility (Nonequilibrium Latent Cycles 2025; Measuring irreversibility from learned representations 2023; LENS 2025) shows learned dynamics can break detailed balance and be time-asymmetric, and the position paper 'Beyond Equilibrium' (2025) argues generative processes are often irreversible—but none connects this to feature-steering controllability of DESIGNS. No prior work (a) tests whether steer-then-unsteer returns a scientific generator to its original design, (b) quantifies steering hysteresis as a controllability-reliability failure, or (c) ties hysteresis magnitude to steer timing and feature geometry. This reframes the ubiquitous assumption of reversible control—distinct from all my prior proposals (compositionality, off-mode reach, side-effect drift), which assume a single forward steer and never study the undo operation.
Abstract: Designers using interpretable-feature steering treat it like a knob: add a feature vector to increase a property, and—implicitly—dial it back or adjust around it if you overshoot. We test whether this reversibility assumption holds for scientific generative models, and find reason to expect it does not. Because generation is a nonlinear, path-dependent process (especially autoregressive decoding and iterative diffusion), a steering perturbation applied partway through generation contaminates every subsequent decision, so removing the steer—or applying the exact opposite steer—need not return the model to where it started. We call this steering hysteresis: the finished object after a steer-then-unsteer cycle differs persistently from the unsteered baseline, leaving unintended 'scars' in properties the designer never touched. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we (1) MEASURE hysteresis via a steer-then-reverse protocol, quantifying residual property drift and sequence/graph distance from baseline after the steer is nominally undone; (2) test whether hysteresis is SYSTEMATIC (stable direction across seeds) rather than sampling noise, using paired controls; (3) INTERPRET the mechanism by testing whether hysteresis magnitude is predicted by how early in generation the steer is applied and by feature-decoder overlap; and (4) AUDIT reliability, showing that the naive undo workflow silently fails and that a simple early-vs-late scheduling fix reduces scars. We predict substantial, systematic, timing-dependent hysteresis, invisible to forward-only steering evaluations—establishing reversibility as a necessary, currently-ignored axis for controllable design.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 at 150M and 650M params (public checkpoints) for proteins; a GPT-style autoregressive SMILES chemical LM (~85M params, trained on the ~1.9M-molecule MOSES corpus, or an equivalent public checkpoint) for molecules. Models are FROZEN; only SAEs/probes are trainable. SAEs: TopK SAE on the residual stream at one layer chosen by an intrinsic-dimension elbow heuristic (plus a second layer for robustness), dictionary width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted only at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. Difference-of-means directions serve as a non-SAE baseline. ORACLES (exact/cheap): proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet content via DSSP on ESMFold structures, GRAVY, molecular weight, motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic count, functional groups (RDKit SMARTS). VALIDITY gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity + synthetic accessibility (molecules); core analyses restricted to reversed objects that remain valid. DISTANCE metrics: sequence identity / edit distance and embedding distance (proteins); Tanimoto / canonical-SMILES match and graph edit distance (molecules). FEATURE BANK: ~30 property-linked features per domain (concept-correlation / probe AUROC on held-out natural objects). Compute: two frozen ESM-2 sizes + one small SMILES LM on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- feature steering leaves a persistent scar; it is not a reversible knob): Tests that steer-then-reverse does not return generation to the unsteered design. Data: from the SAME initial condition (fixed seed / masked template / prompt), 500 matched triplets per feature per domain, features drawn from the bank. Each triplet: (A) unsteered baseline, (B) steer forward with feature f at strength s for part of generation, (C) steer-then-reverse -- apply +s then, after a switch point, either drop the vector ("remove") or apply -s ("symmetric reverse"); both reversal modes are run and reported separately (not assumed equivalent). Decisive metric first: PERSISTENT-FRACTION = fraction of the forward property change (B vs A) that remains in C vs A on the TARGET property; then off-target scar magnitude across the full off-target oracle battery; then object distance (identity / Tanimoto) between C and A. Convincing: median persistent-fraction >= 0.2 with a paired test clearing Experiment 2's noise floor, for a majority of features in both domains. Undecidable band: persistent-fraction in [0.05, 0.15) and within the noise floor -> not distinguishable from reversible; report as no-scar. Negative result (persistent-fraction < 0.05, off-target scar within noise): steering IS reversible -- a clean, publishable positive result validating the undo/adjust workflow.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the hysteresis is systematic, not sampling noise): Tests that scars exceed stochastic drift and point in a consistent direction. Noise floor: 500 pairs of independent UNSTEERED runs from seed-perturbed initial conditions per domain, giving the baseline property/distance spread. Decisive metric first: standardized effect size of steer-then-reverse persistent-fraction ABOVE the noise floor (Cohen's d), then residual-DIRECTION consistency across seeds (cosine of the C-minus-A property/embedding shift, tested against a matched-norm random-direction control) via a mixed-effects model with CIs. Convincing: d >= 0.8 above floor AND mean residual-direction cosine >= 0.3 with CI excluding 0. Undecidable band: d in [0.2, 0.5) OR direction cosine CI overlapping [−0.1, 0.1] -> scar not separable from noise; H1 is downgraded to "not established". Negative result (d < 0.2): hysteresis is indistinguishable from sampling noise -- reported as reversibility.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- hysteresis is larger for iterative/autoregressive generation): Tests that an early perturbation contaminates downstream decisions more in sequential generation. Systems compared: autoregressive SMILES generation and autoregressive vs masked-infilling ESM-2 protein generation, versus a near-instantaneous single-step steer as a low-hysteresis control. Decisive metric first: persistent-fraction (and off-target scar) for iterative/autoregressive vs single-step generation at matched forward property gain. Convincing: iterative/autoregressive persistent-fraction exceeds the single-step control by an effect size d >= 0.5, and autoregressive exceeds masked-infilling. Undecidable band: d in [0.1, 0.3) -> generation-mode dependence present but weak; report, do not headline. Negative result (d < 0.1 or reversed sign): hysteresis is not driven by sequential contamination -- refines the mechanism claim and is reported as such.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- scar magnitude is predicted by steer earliness and feature-decoder overlap): Tests the two named predictors. Design: sweep the SWITCH POINT across >=5 positions from early to late in generation, and for each feature compute feature-decoder overlap (cosine of f's decoder direction with other property directions). Decisive metric first: out-of-sample R^2 of a regressor predicting per-steer persistent-fraction from {switch-point, feature-decoder overlap}, compared against a concept-correlation-only baseline (nested-model comparison). Convincing: the two predictors reach R^2 >= 0.3 and add >= 0.1 R^2 over concept-correlation, with earlier switch points and higher overlap both associated with larger scars (signs as hypothesized, CIs excluding 0). Undecidable band: predictor R^2 in [0.1, 0.2) or added-R^2 in [0.03, 0.1) -> weak predictors; report coefficients, withhold the predictive claim. Negative result (added-R^2 < 0.03): earliness/overlap do not predict scars -- the hypothesized mechanism is unsupported; report which alternative correlates (e.g., strength) if any.

Experiment 5 (payoff -- forward-only evaluation misses hysteresis, and a scheduling fix reduces it): Tests the "silently unreliable" claim and a mitigation. Blind spot: decisive metric first -- correlation between forward property gain/validity (B vs A) and residual scar (C vs A); convincing if |r| <= 0.2 (a "successful" steer carries no signal about its scar). Mitigation: apply/remove the steer only within a late causal window (or ramp strength); decisive metric -- scar reduction at MATCHED forward property gain, tracing a control-vs-reversibility frontier. Convincing: >= 30% scar reduction at matched gain. Undecidable band: forward-vs-scar |r| in [0.2, 0.4) (blind spot partial) or scar reduction in [10%, 30%) (fix marginal) -> report the frontier without a strong claim. Negative result: forward metrics already predict scars (|r| > 0.4) or the fix gives <10% reduction -- the workflow is not silently unreliable / the fix does not help, reported honestly.

Experiment 6 (robustness of H1-H4): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, autoregressive vs masked-infilling protein generation, TopK vs difference-of-means directions, two layers, and >=3 properties per domain; report the fraction of cells where hysteresis, its systematicity, the generation-mode effect, and the predictors replicate. A result stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles (ESMFold, DSSP, RDKit, HMMER) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal controllability and design reproducibility, not experimental function—stated explicitly. 2) Generation is inherently stochastic, so distinguishing hysteresis from sampling noise is essential; we mitigate with a carefully matched noise-floor baseline (independent unsteered runs), paired same-seed comparisons, direction-consistency tests, and random-direction controls—if hysteresis does not exceed the floor, that is itself a clean, publishable positive result establishing that steering IS reversible. 3) 'Remove steer' vs 'symmetric reverse' may behave differently; we report both rather than assume equivalence. 4) Hysteresis could be trivially explained by validity collapse; we restrict core analysis to the regime where reversed objects remain valid and report scars separately. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound both scar and geometry; controlled with multiple SAE variants, layers, and difference-of-means baselines. 6) The timing/geometry predictors may be property- or model-specific; we test multiple properties, sizes, and generation modes and report where they fail. 7) The scheduling fix may reduce forward property gain; we quantify the control-vs-reversibility tradeoff rather than assume a free lunch.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) steer-then-unsteer in scientific generative models leaves persistent residual changes (“hysteresis/scars”); (2) this is systematic, not just sampling noise; (3) magnitude depends on steer timing and feature-decoder geometry; (4) a scheduling fix can reduce scars; (5) the novelty is mainly in the problem framing/measurement, plus a mechanism claim, not a new method. Name: oracle_transfer_gap_steering
Title: Steering to the Judge, Not the Property: Does Interpretable-Feature Control of Scientific Designs Survive a Change of Oracle?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering produces property gains that are partly an artifact of the specific in-silico oracle used to guide/evaluate it: a large fraction of the measured gain evaporates when the SAME steered objects are scored by an independent, more trustworthy oracle. We hypothesize this 'oracle-transfer gap' is systematic (worse at higher steering strength, worse for oracles that share features with the steered model), and that a cheap, intervention-free internal signature—the alignment of the steering direction with oracle-agnostic physicochemical features versus oracle-specific idiosyncrasy—predicts which steers will transfer across oracles.
Related Work: Text-LLM steering studies establish that steering is fragile and trades off with capability (Mind the Performance Gap 2026; The Rogue Scalpel 2025; 'When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins' 2026), that interpretability weakly predicts steering utility (Does Higher Interpretability Imply Better Utility 2025), and that steering reliability has geometric predictors (Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors 2026). Scientific interpretability-of-generation work (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025) reports property GAINS measured by a single in-silico oracle and never asks whether those gains are oracle-dependent artifacts. Sim-to-real work (Intervention Design for Sim2Real 2020; SourceNet 2026) studies train/deploy domain gaps for predictors, not steering-of-generators. My own prior proposals each audit one property class against one better oracle; NONE isolates the general, cross-domain phenomenon that a steering-induced gain is contingent on the CHOICE of measuring oracle, quantifies how much survives an oracle swap, or identifies an internal signature predicting oracle-robustness. This reframes steering reliability as a MEASUREMENT-TRANSFER problem: the danger is not overshoot but that the model steers toward the quirks of whatever judge scored it.
Abstract: Interpretable-feature steering is judged almost universally by one number: an in-silico oracle says the target property increased. But scientific properties are measured by many imperfect instruments, and a control method that genuinely changed the property should look good to any competent judge. We test whether steering-induced gains are robust to a change of oracle, or whether steering silently optimizes the idiosyncrasies of the specific judge that guided it—an 'oracle-transfer gap.' Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we steer property-linked features and, crucially, score the SAME steered objects with multiple independent oracles per property (e.g., for hydrophobicity/logP: distinct empirical estimators; for stability: a learned head vs a physics-based estimator; for structure content: DSSP-on-ESMFold vs an alternative predictor). We (1) quantify the oracle-transfer gap = fraction of the guiding-oracle gain that vanishes under an independent oracle, and its dose-response with steering strength; (2) test whether the gap is larger when the guiding oracle shares representational features with the steered model (feature leakage) than for a physics-based judge; (3) LOCATE and validate an intervention-free robustness signature—the projection of the steering direction onto oracle-agnostic physicochemical features vs oracle-specific directions—that predicts per-steer transfer; and (4) deploy a robustness-gated / multi-oracle-orthogonalized steering controller that keeps only oracle-invariant gains. We predict substantial, systematic oracle-transfer gaps invisible to single-oracle evaluation, a cheap predictor of robust steers, and a simple recipe for control that generalizes across judges.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (public checkpoints); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M params, MOSES-trained or equivalent public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. ORACLE PANELS (>=3 independent oracles per target property, each measuring the same physical quantity by different means): molecules -- logP via Crippen/RDKit vs an ML logP model vs a group-contribution estimator; size via exact MW vs a learned descriptor; polarity via TPSA vs an empirical solubility model. Proteins -- hydrophobicity via GRAVY vs a learned head; secondary-structure content via DSSP-on-ESMFold vs an alternative structure predictor; stability via a fine-tuned ML head vs a physics-based (FoldX/Rosetta-style) estimator. Each oracle is pre-labeled "model-adjacent" (learned, may share features with the LM's training signal) or "physics-based" (mechanistic, independent). PRECONDITION: report inter-oracle agreement on ~2,000 NATURAL held-out objects per domain first, to bound the gap expected from oracle noise alone, and report pairwise oracle correlations so gaps are read relative to oracle independence. VALIDITY gates: RDKit-validity + SA (molecules), ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins); core analysis restricted to valid objects. FEATURE BANK: ~30-50 property-linked SAE features per domain, selected by concept-correlation / probe AUROC against the panel-AVERAGE (not one oracle), plus difference-of-means baselines. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + lightweight oracle models on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- steering gains partly evaporate under an independent oracle: the oracle-transfer gap exists): Tests that a large fraction of measured gain does not transfer to held-out oracles scoring the SAME objects. Design: for each feature designate one panel member as the GUIDING oracle (rotated across members to avoid single-oracle idiosyncrasy), sweep steering strength (6 levels), generate 200 objects per level, and score every object under the guiding oracle AND every held-out panel oracle. Decisive metric first: ORACLE-TRANSFER GAP = 1 - (mean held-out-oracle gain)/(guiding-oracle gain); then SILENT-OVERCLAIM RATE = fraction of steers judged successful by the guiding oracle but not by the panel majority. Baseline to subtract: the gap expected from natural-object inter-oracle disagreement (precondition). Convincing: mean transfer gap >= 0.3 above the natural-object baseline, and silent-overclaim rate >= 0.2, with matched-non-property-feature and random-direction controls near 0. Undecidable band: transfer gap in [0.1, 0.3) above baseline OR silent-overclaim in [0.1, 0.2) -> gap present but modest; report magnitude, do not headline. Negative result (gap < 0.1 above baseline): gains transfer cleanly -- a valuable positive result that interpretable steering targets genuine physics, not judge idiosyncrasy.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap is systematic: it grows with steering strength): Tests the dose-response of the gap. Uses Experiment 1's strength sweep. Decisive metric first: slope of transfer gap vs steering strength (per-feature, mixed-effects, CIs), then whether the SILENT-OVERCLAIM RATE rises with strength. Convincing: positive slope with CI excluding 0 for a majority of features, gap at the highest strength >= 1.5x the gap at the lowest. Undecidable band: slope CI overlapping 0 but point estimate positive, or high/low ratio in [1.1, 1.5) -> weak dose-dependence; report. Negative result (flat or negative slope): the gap is strength-independent -- refines H1 (a fixed oracle bias rather than optimization-driven overfitting).

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the gap is worse when guiding with a model-adjacent oracle than a physics-based one): Tests the feature-leakage prediction. Systems compared: guiding with model-adjacent vs physics-based panel members, at matched steering budget. Decisive metric first: difference in transfer gap between the two guiding-oracle classes (mixed-effects effect size, CIs). Also show the blind spot: correlation between validity/pseudo-perplexity/guiding-oracle confidence and the true transfer gap (hypothesis |r| <= 0.2). Convincing: model-adjacent gap exceeds physics-based gap by effect size d >= 0.5 with CI excluding 0, and blind-spot |r| <= 0.2. Undecidable band: d in [0.1, 0.3) or blind-spot |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> weak leakage effect; report. Negative result (d < 0.1): the gap is not larger for model-adjacent oracles -- the feature-leakage mechanism is unsupported, reported honestly.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- an intervention-free oracle-agnostic-alignment signature predicts which steers transfer): Tests the predictor. For each steering direction compute (a) projection onto an ORACLE-AGNOSTIC subspace (features predicting the property consistently across ALL panel oracles) vs ORACLE-SPECIFIC directions (predicting only the guiding oracle's residual after removing panel consensus), (b) decoder-direction overlap, (c) concept-correlation. Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / out-of-sample R^2 of per-steer transfer gap regressed on oracle-agnostic-alignment, compared against a concept-correlation baseline; then precision@k for selecting oracle-robust steers as a pre-flight filter, then compute saved by skipping non-transferring steers before running the full panel. Convincing: oracle-agnostic-alignment reaches |rho| >= 0.5 and adds >= 0.1 R^2 over concept-correlation, precision@10 >= 0.7. Undecidable band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) or added-R^2 in [0.03, 0.1) -> weak predictor; report, withhold the pre-flight claim. Negative result (|rho| < 0.2, added-R^2 < 0.03): the internal signature does not predict transfer -- the predictor contribution is withdrawn, leaving the phenomenon (Experiment 1) as the result.

Experiment 5 (mitigation -- consensus-aligned steering keeps robust gain): Tests whether steering along the oracle-CONSENSUS subspace (or gating out low-agnostic-alignment steers) Pareto-dominates naive single-oracle steering. Systems compared: consensus-aligned vs naive steering on a gain-vs-transfer frontier. Decisive metric first: consensus (panel-majority) property gain retained at matched validity, then transfer gap, then novelty/diversity. Convincing: consensus-aligned steering retains >= 70% of naive robust gain while cutting the transfer gap by >= 30% at matched validity (Pareto improvement). Undecidable band: robust-gain retention in [50%, 70%) or gap reduction in [10%, 30%) -> partial improvement; report the frontier. Negative result: consensus steering loses > half the robust gain or does not shrink the gap -- no free mitigation; report the tradeoff.

Experiment 6 (robustness of H1-H4): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, and all target properties; report which properties show the largest transfer gaps and the fraction of cells where the gap, its dose-response, the model-adjacent effect, and the predictor replicate. Also report sensitivity to panel size (drop one oracle, re-estimate the consensus). A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as property-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) All oracles are in-silico; the claim is deliberately about ROBUSTNESS ACROSS INDEPENDENT JUDGES, not wet-lab truth—but a gain that fails to transfer across competent oracles is prima facie untrustworthy, and a physics-based panel member reduces circularity. We report the panel's inter-oracle agreement on NATURAL objects first to bound expected gap from oracle noise alone. 2) Some panel oracles may themselves be biased/correlated, shrinking apparent gaps; we choose maximally mechanistically-distinct oracles and report their pairwise correlation so the gap is interpreted relative to oracle independence. 3) The transfer gap could partly reflect validity collapse rather than oracle-specific optimization; we restrict core analysis to valid objects and report the gap separately. 4) The robustness predictor may be property- or model-specific; we test multiple properties, sizes, and SAE variants and report where it fails. 5) Defining the 'oracle-agnostic subspace' depends on the panel; a richer panel gives a cleaner consensus—we quantify sensitivity to panel size. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, difference-of-means baselines, and random-direction controls. 7) If gains transfer cleanly across oracles (small gap), that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable-feature steering targets genuine physics rather than judge idiosyncrasy.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) define and measure an 'oracle-transfer gap' for steering-induced property gains on the same generated objects; (2) show this gap is systematic with steering strength and oracle type; (3) propose an internal oracle-agnostic alignment signature that predicts transfer; (4) use consensus/orthogonalized steering as a mitigation. The closest prior family is single-oracle interpretability-of-generation plus reward-hacking/sim2real gap work; the actual delta is cross-oracle evaluation of steering, not just single-judge gains. This is a non-trivial next step and plausibly a new phenomenon in steering-of-generators, though parts are an adaptation of Goodhart/reward-misspecification ideas.

Name: locality_count_generalization_design
Title: More Motifs Than Ever Seen: Does Conditional Score Locality Govern Count Generalization in Scientific Generative Design?
Short Hypothesis: Scientific generative models can design objects with MORE independent functional elements (motifs, catalytic sites, functional groups) than appeared in any training example ('count generalization') only when their internal conditional computation is LOCAL — i.e., each element's placement depends on a spatially/sequentially sparse neighborhood rather than the global configuration. We hypothesize (i) count generalization succeeds or fails per model/property, (ii) an intervention-free locality signature of the element-placement feature predicts which case holds, and (iii) causally enforcing locality (masking non-local dependencies of the placement feature) unlocks count generalization that a non-local model otherwise fails, at preserved validity.
Related Work: A recent line proves that compositional/length generalization in conditional diffusion models is equivalent to 'local conditional scores' (sparse pixel and conditioner dependencies) and shows a causal locality intervention restores length generalization in CLEVR/image models (Local Mechanisms of Compositional Generalization, 2025; Kamb & Ganguli 2024; Niedoba 2024). Compositional-generalization theory (kernel theory 2024; identifiability/object-centric 2023; complexity-based compositionality 2024) and disentanglement-for-C-OoD work (CLIP 2024, data-diversity 2025) all study this in vision/text. Separately, scientific-model interpretability (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; ProtoMech 2026; Circuits/Features/Heuristics in Molecular Transformers 2025) discovers and steers features for single-element properties but NEVER studies count generalization, never measures conditional-score locality, and never tests locality as its causal mechanism. My prior proposals audit compositional INTERFERENCE and off-mode reach but assume a fixed target count and never touch the locality-count-generalization link. This proposal is the first to (a) transfer the locality<->count-generalization theory into scientific sequence/graph design, (b) measure conditional locality of interpretable element-placement features, and (c) causally enforce locality to unlock designs exceeding training element counts — a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism claim in a high-stakes domain.
Abstract: Real scientific design frequently demands packing MORE independent functional elements into one object than nature or the training set ever showed: an enzyme with several catalytic sites, a protein with multiple binding motifs, a molecule with many decorated functional groups. Whether generative models can do this — 'count generalization' — and why, is unknown. Recent theory for conditional diffusion proves that compositional/length generalization is equivalent to conditional score LOCALITY: each element's placement depending on a sparse local neighborhood rather than the global configuration. We transfer this theory into scientific design and test it mechanistically. Using protein language models (ESM-2), a SMILES chemical language model, and a masked-diffusion protein/molecule generator with sparse autoencoders, we (1) LOCATE interpretable element-placement features (features that fire when a motif/functional group is instantiated) and measure their CONDITIONAL LOCALITY — how sparsely each placement depends on distant positions/other elements, via ablation of distal context and Jacobian sparsity; (2) establish the count-generalization PHENOMENON by requesting objects with k functional elements for k beyond the training-count support and measuring valid success against hard oracles (HMMER/regex motifs, RDKit SMARTS); (3) TEST the hypothesis that locality predicts count-generalization success across models/properties; and (4) CAUSALLY ENFORCE locality — masking the placement feature's non-local dependencies during generation — and test whether it unlocks higher-count valid designs that the unmodified (non-local) model fails, at preserved validity. Results would give a mechanistic, actionable principle for pushing scientific generators past their training element counts.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint); and, for the causal locality intervention that needs per-step conditional scores, a masked-diffusion generator with accessible per-step activations -- a discrete diffusion protein LM (DPLM/EvoDiff-style, public) and a masked discrete-diffusion molecule model (DiGress/masked-SMILES-style). All generators FROZEN; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK on residual-stream / denoiser activations at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. ELEMENT oracles (exact, countable): proteins -- discrete motif instances (zinc fingers, catalytic-triad-like motifs, specified short motifs) via HMMER/regex, counted per sequence; molecules -- functional-group instances via specified SMARTS (hydroxyls, halogens, aromatic rings), counted per molecule. VALIDITY gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity + SA (molecules). PRECONDITION: from the training corpus, record the DISTRIBUTION of element counts per object (the training-count support and its max), so "beyond training count" is well-defined per element type. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + two public diffusion generators on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- count generalization succeeds or fails, per model and property): Tests that some (model, element) pairs generate valid objects with MORE independent elements than any training example while others break down. Data: for each element type, request k elements for k spanning within-support up to beyond the training-max count, via three elicitation methods (count-conditioned prompting, iterative element insertion, feature-steered placement); generate 300 objects per k. Decisive metric first: VALID-COUNT-SUCCESS(k) = fraction of generations containing EXACTLY k valid, correctly-formed elements AND passing validity gates; then the count-generalization BOUNDARY = largest k with valid-success >= 0.5, normalized by training-max count; then the SILENT-COUNT-FAILURE profile (wrong count / degenerate / invalid). Random-count and unconditioned controls. Convincing existence of both regimes: at least one (model, element) pair has boundary/training-max >= 1.2 (genuine extrapolation) and at least one has boundary/training-max <= 1.0 (breakdown), each with valid-success curves separated from the unconditioned control. Undecidable band: boundary/training-max in [1.0, 1.2) -> extrapolation not clearly beyond training support; report as "at-support", not generalization. Negative result (no pair exceeds 1.0): no count generalization anywhere -- H2/H3 become vacuous; reported as a null with the failure profile.

Experiment 2 (locate element-placement features and measure their conditional locality): Prerequisite measurement for H2/H3. Identify SAE features that fire at the instantiation of each target element (concept-correlation / probe AUROC on held-out objects, localized to the element positions; retain features with AUROC >= 0.7). For each placement feature compute a LOCALITY score from (a) distal-context ablation -- change in the feature's activation / placement decision when distant positions and other already-placed elements are ablated/shuffled (local features barely change), and (b) Jacobian sparsity -- the spatial/sequential decay profile of the placement-logit gradient (a locality radius). Decisive metric: per-feature locality score with test-retest reliability across seeds >= 0.7 (else the score is too noisy to use as a predictor and is reported as such).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- an intervention-free locality signature predicts which pairs generalize): Tests that locality predicts the count-generalization boundary. Across element types, models, and two layers, regress the normalized boundary (Experiment 1) on the placement feature's locality score (Experiment 2). Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / out-of-sample R^2 of boundary on locality, compared against concept-correlation and single-element steerability baselines (nested-model comparison), then reported per-property and pooled. Convincing: higher locality predicts larger boundary with |rho| >= 0.5 and adds >= 0.1 R^2 over both baselines, CIs excluding 0. Undecidable band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) or added-R^2 in [0.03, 0.1) -> weak predictor; report coefficients, withhold the claim. Negative result (|rho| < 0.2, added-R^2 < 0.03): locality does not track count generalization -- an informative refutation pointing to an alternative cause (e.g., data-count diversity), reported with whatever does correlate.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- causally enforcing locality unlocks count generalization a non-local model otherwise fails): The mechanism test, run on the masked-diffusion generator (conditional scores directly accessible). Pick a (model, element) pair that FAILS count generalization (Experiment 1) and whose placement feature is measured NON-local (Experiment 2). Intervene: at each denoising step, mask the placement feature's dependence on distal positions / other-element features, restricting its effective receptive field to the measured local radius. Decisive metric first: count-generalization gain = increase in valid-count-success beyond the training-max count vs the unmodified model, then validity retention, then whether the radius that works matches the Location-measured radius. Controls: enforcing locality on a random non-placement feature (should not help), a model already local (should be unaffected), matched-norm random masking. Convincing: valid-count-success beyond training-max rises by >= 0.2 absolute over the unmodified model at validity retained within 5% of baseline, controls show no such gain, and the effective radius matches the measured one within a factor of 2. Undecidable band: gain in [0.05, 0.2) absolute OR validity drop in [5%, 15%) -> partial/costly unlock; report the count-vs-validity frontier. Negative result (gain < 0.05 or validity drop > 15%): enforcing locality does not unlock generalization -- refutes the causal claim; report whether the failure is implementation fidelity (measured and stated) or genuine.

Experiment 5 (robustness / boundary of H2-H3): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, autoregressive vs masked-diffusion generation, and >=3 element types, stratifying by element independence (well-separated vs coupled elements). Report where locality<->count-generalization holds vs breaks, the fraction of cells replicating, and whether the link is stronger for physically independent elements (where non-locality is not required) than coupled ones. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as element-class-specific rather than general.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles (HMMER/regex, RDKit SMARTS, ESMFold) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal count controllability and its locality mechanism, not experimental viability — stated explicitly. Element COUNTS, however, are exact/objective structural facts, which strengthens the core measurement. 2) The causal-locality-enforcement intervention (masking distal dependencies of a feature) is nontrivial to implement cleanly, especially for autoregressive models; we focus the causal test on the masked-diffusion generator where conditional scores are directly accessible (matching the source theory) and treat autoregressive results as corroborating, reporting implementation fidelity. 3) The locality<->count-generalization link may hold for physically-independent elements but fail for coupled ones (where non-locality is genuinely required); we stratify by element independence and report this as an informative boundary rather than a failure. 4) Count-conditioned generation may be hard to elicit; we use three elicitation methods (prompting, iterative insertion, feature-steered placement) and report the strongest fair comparison. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound both locality measurement and placement-feature identification; controlled with multiple layers, difference-of-means baselines, raw-activation probes, and random-feature controls. 6) If count generalization does NOT track locality (e.g., it is driven by data-count diversity instead), that is itself a valuable, publishable result adapting/refuting the diffusion-locality theory for scientific design and pointing to data diversity as the operative cause. 7) A positive causal result would provide a concrete, cheap recipe (locality masking) for exceeding training element counts — high practical value if it holds.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) count generalization in scientific sequence/graph design; (2) an interpretable element-placement feature shows measurable conditional locality; (3) locality predicts the max-count boundary; (4) causal masking of non-local dependencies unlocks higher-count generation; (5) the effect is tested across proteins/molecules and autoregressive/masked-diffusion settings. The main theory is not new: the proposal directly imports the prior locality<->generalization result from conditional diffusion. The novelty is in the transfer to ML4Science, the interpretable-feature measurement, and the causal intervention test in a new domain. That is more than a trivial baseline extension, but still clearly derivative of the cited theory family rather than a new mechanism family.

Name: epistemic_selfsignal_design
Title: Does the Generator Know It's Guessing? An Internal Epistemic Self-Signal That Governs Design Quality in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Scientific sequence/graph generative models carry a compact, interpretable INTERNAL EPISTEMIC self-signal during generation that encodes how uncertain the model is about the object it is producing, and—mirroring the shared uncertainty/correctness circuits found in text LLMs (SCIURus)—this self-signal is causally SHARED with actual design quality: it fires low exactly when the finished object is novel/out-of-distribution and low-quality (unfoldable, invalid, off-property), it is better calibrated than output likelihood/perplexity, and steering it changes both the model's internal confidence and the true quality of generated designs together.
Related Work: Two literatures meet for the first time. (1) Text-LLM internal-uncertainty work shows models 'know what they know': SCIURus (2025) finds factuality and uncertainty share the same circuits; 'Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict OOD Behaviors' (2025) shows causal internal features predict correctness under shift; 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) and P(IK)-probe work map self-knowledge features. ALL are in text and concern factual QA, not generation of scientific objects. (2) Scientific interpretability-of-generation (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; chemistry-LM SAEs 2025; single-cell SAEs 2024) discovers/steers features for TARGET PROPERTIES and never studies whether the generator internally represents its own epistemic uncertainty about the object it is building, nor whether that self-signal is causally tied to design quality. Molecular-OOD work (MOOD 2024) shows external PREDICTOR calibration collapses under covariate shift but says nothing about a GENERATOR's internal self-signal. No prior work (a) locates an internal epistemic self-signal inside a scientific generator, (b) tests whether it is a shared circuit with true design quality (the SCIURus phenomenon transferred to a new, high-stakes object class where quality is objectively verifiable), or (c) uses it as a calibrated, causally-validated confidence readout for design. This is distinct from all my prior proposals, which audit controllability of a specific property; here the object of study is the model's self-knowledge and its causal link to quality.
Abstract: Generative models for proteins and molecules routinely emit confident-looking designs that are actually invalid, unfoldable, or property-wrong—especially in the novel, out-of-distribution regions where design is most valuable. In text language models, recent work shows that uncertainty and correctness are computed by shared internal circuits: the model 'knows what it knows.' We ask whether scientific generators possess an analogous internal epistemic self-signal during generation, whether it is causally shared with the true quality of the object being produced, and whether it can serve as a calibrated confidence readout that output likelihood cannot. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders, we (1) LOCATE candidate epistemic self-signal features by probing intermediate activations for how novel/OOD and how ultimately-valid the object being generated is, verified by hard oracles (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity, RDKit-validity) and novelty measures (identity/Tanimoto to the training set); (2) test the SHARED-CIRCUIT hypothesis via causal ablation and patching—does perturbing the located self-signal move BOTH the model's internal confidence AND the true design quality together, as SCIURus finds for text?; (3) evaluate the self-signal as a CALIBRATED confidence readout, comparing its ability to flag low-quality/OOD designs against likelihood, perplexity, and a black-box activation probe; and (4) deploy it as an epistemic-gated generation controller that abstains or resamples on low-confidence designs, measuring valid-yield-per-compute. We predict a genuine, shared, better-calibrated self-signal—recasting interpretability as a source of trustworthy design confidence.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. QUALITY oracles (hard): proteins -- ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity + non-degeneracy (foldable & valid); molecules -- RDKit-validity + SA + non-degeneracy. NOVELTY/OOD: identity/edit distance to nearest training protein (mmseqs2/BLAST) or Tanimoto nearest-neighbour distance to nearest training molecule. CORPUS: generate ~20,000 objects per model spanning in-distribution (typical sampling) and OOD (high-temperature, steered-off-mode, rare-scaffold-conditioned) regimes so quality and novelty both vary widely; split 70/15/15 into probe-train / val / test by generation seed (no object leakage). Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + ESMFold on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a compact interpretable epistemic self-signal is decodable mid-generation): Tests that a small internal feature set predicts eventual quality and novelty before the object is finished. At generation-progress fractions {0.25, 0.5, 0.75}, probe SAE features and raw activations to predict (a) eventual design quality (valid vs invalid/low) and (b) novelty/OOD-ness, selecting a compact self-signal feature set by information-based selection. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC for eventual quality at each progress fraction (established BEFORE the object is complete), then R^2 for novelty, then whether the SAME features predict both (a first sign of sharing), against a raw-activation-probe baseline. Convincing: at progress <=0.5, quality AUROC >= 0.75 from a compact feature set (<=32 features) and the same set predicts novelty with AUROC >= 0.7. Undecidable band: quality AUROC in [0.6, 0.7) at 0.5 progress -> a self-signal exists but is weak/late; report, do not headline the "compact early" claim. Negative result (quality AUROC < 0.6 at all pre-completion fractions): no decodable epistemic self-signal exists -- a clean negative that scientific generators do not "know what they know", and H2-H4 are reported as not applicable.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the self-signal is causally SHARED with true design quality, not merely correlated): Tests the shared-circuit prediction (SCIURus analog). Ablate/patch the located self-signal features and measure whether BOTH the internal confidence read-out (self-signal value / P(valid) probe) AND the TRUE finished-object oracle quality move together; conversely patch self-signal activations from high-confidence into low-confidence generations. Decisive metric first: confidence-quality COUPLING = correlation between the intervention-induced change in internal confidence and the change in oracle quality across a dose sweep; then specificity -- ablating a pure target-property feature must NOT move the epistemic signal, and random-direction / matched-property-feature controls must NOT couple confidence and quality. Convincing: coupling r >= 0.5 (CI excluding 0) under the epistemic ablation, patching high->low confidence raises BOTH internal confidence and oracle quality, and controls show coupling |r| <= 0.2 (specific). Undecidable band: coupling r in [0.2, 0.4) OR controls also show |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> coupling present but not clearly specific; report as suggestive. Negative result (coupling |r| < 0.2, or controls couple as strongly): the signal is not a shared correctness circuit -- reported as a non-specific/absent result, distinguishing "detects novelty" from "predicts quality".

Experiment 3 (H3 -- the self-signal is better calibrated than output likelihood/perplexity, especially OOD): Tests calibration as a confidence read-out. Systems compared: intervention-free self-signal (read mid-generation) vs generation likelihood, pseudo-perplexity/token-entropy, RDKit/validity heuristics, and a black-box raw-activation probe. Decisive metric first: calibration ECE for flagging invalid/off-property/novel-but-broken designs, then AUROC, both STRATIFIED by novelty (in-distribution vs OOD tertiles). Convincing: in the OOD tertile the self-signal keeps ECE <= 0.1 and AUROC >= 0.75 while likelihood/perplexity degrade to AUROC <= 0.65 (a >= 0.1 AUROC advantage where output-side signals fail, mirroring predictor-calibration collapse on novel inputs). Undecidable band: OOD self-signal-minus-likelihood AUROC gap in [0.0, 0.05] -> no calibration advantage; report parity. Negative result (self-signal ECE > 0.2 OOD or no advantage over likelihood): the internal signal is not better calibrated -- the calibration contribution is withdrawn.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- gating/steering the self-signal changes true design quality; an epistemic-gated controller pays off): Tests that acting on the self-signal moves real quality and yields a usable controller. Deploy the self-signal as a generation-time gate (abstain/resample when internal confidence is low); sweep the threshold. Decisive metric first: valid+in-quality objects per unit compute (a valid-yield-per-compute frontier) vs run-to-completion, likelihood/perplexity gating, and a black-box-probe gate; then false-abort rate; then diversity/novelty retention (guard against collapse to memorized in-distribution outputs). Convincing: the self-signal gate dominates likelihood gating on valid-yield-per-compute by >= 20% at matched false-abort rate, with novelty retention within 10% of run-to-completion. Undecidable band: valid-yield improvement in [5%, 20%) or novelty loss in [10%, 25%) -> a modest/costly controller; report the frontier. Negative result (improvement < 5% or novelty loss > 25%): gating on the self-signal does not help beyond output-side signals -- reported honestly; the phenomenon (Experiments 1-3) stands or falls on its own.

Experiment 5 (interpretation + robustness of H1-H4): Auto-label the self-signal features (max-activating partial generations -- do they fire on frustrated partial folds / chemically inconsistent prefixes?). Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, and two layers; report the fraction of cells where the self-signal, the shared-circuit coupling, and the OOD-calibration advantage replicate, and whether coupling weakens for subtle vs gross failures. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico quality oracles (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal epistemic self-knowledge and design reliability, not experimental viability—stated explicitly. 2) The shared-circuit claim requires distinguishing genuine coupling from a trivial 'ablation breaks everything' artifact; we mitigate with random-direction and matched-property-feature controls, and a specificity test that property-feature ablation leaves the epistemic signal intact while epistemic-signal ablation couples confidence and quality—if coupling is non-specific, we report that as a negative result. 3) The self-signal may merely track OOD-ness rather than a genuine correctness representation; the novelty-stratified calibration test and the causal coupling test separate 'detects novelty' from 'predicts quality', and both are informative. 4) An internal SAE-based self-signal might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; even so, interpretability (naming what the signal fires on), the shared-circuit causal finding, and the OOD-calibration/compute-saving payoff are the contributions, reported honestly. 5) Gating could bias outputs toward memorized in-distribution designs; we explicitly measure diversity/novelty retention. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes, and random-direction controls. 7) If no shared, better-calibrated self-signal exists, that is a clean, publishable negative result establishing that scientific generators—unlike text LLMs—do NOT 'know what they know' about their own designs, a safety-relevant finding.

Name: dimensional_consistency_blindspot_symbolic_regression
Title: Right Numbers, Wrong Units: Do Neural Symbolic-Regression Models Represent Dimensional Consistency, or Fit Numbers That Silently Violate the Laws of Physics?
Short Hypothesis: Transformer-based neural symbolic-regression (NSR) models possess interpretable, causally-steerable internal features for the NUMERICAL fit of a candidate equation (how well it matches data), but do NOT possess a compact, causally-steerable internal representation of DIMENSIONAL CONSISTENCY — the requirement that added/equated terms carry matching physical units. Consequently, steering a feature to improve numerical fit silently produces dimensionally invalid equations (adding a length to a time, taking log of a dimensioned quantity), a blind spot that R^2/accuracy checks miss but an exact unit-checking oracle exposes; and an intervention-free internal dimensional-consistency signal flags it.
Related Work: Transformer/generative symbolic regression is mature: SymbolicGPT (2021), DGSR (2023), DiffuSR (2025), Controllable NSR / NSRwH (2023, which conditions on hypothesized STRUCTURE but not units), and LaSR (2024, learned concept library). Mechanistic interpretability has JUST reached this domain: PATCHES (2026) discovers operator-generating circuits in an SR transformer and finds probing/DLA capture correlational not causal features; closed-form-gradient interpretation (2024) reads symbolic concepts from latent neurons. Separately, dimensional analysis / units-aware discovery is known to matter (Buckingham-Pi-constrained SR, physics-informed SR like StruSR 2025, domain-prior SR 2025), and dimensional consistency is a HARD, exactly-checkable physical law that most black-box SR ignores. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether a neural SR model INTERNALLY represents dimensional consistency as a causal, steerable feature, contrasts fit-steerability against unit-steerability, surfaces the phenomenon that improving fit silently breaks units, or provides an internal dimensional audit. This introduces the numerical-fit vs physical-law-consistency axis into interpretability-of-generation for symbolic/mathematical objects — a genuinely new object class relative to my prior protein/molecule/DNA/RNA/crystal/reaction/cell proposals — and turns dimensional analysis (an exact oracle) into a mechanism-and-audit target. It also directly answers PATCHES's call to treat SR as a high-potential interpretability domain, by moving from operator circuits to a physically-meaningful invariant.
Abstract: Symbolic regression promises interpretable governing equations from data, and neural symbolic-regression (NSR) transformers now generate candidate equations directly. But a valid physical law must be dimensionally consistent: you cannot add a length to a time, and log/exp require dimensionless arguments. We ask a mechanistic question no prior work addresses: do NSR models internally represent dimensional consistency as a causal, steerable feature the way they represent numerical fit, or do they optimize numbers while silently violating units? We surface a behavioral phenomenon we call the dimensional blind spot: steering an interpretable feature to improve numerical fit reliably lowers error while pushing the generated equation toward dimensional inconsistency — invisible to R^2/accuracy checks but exposed exactly by unit-checking. Dimensional consistency is the ideal testbed because it is an exact, free, symbolic oracle (propagate SI dimensions through the expression tree; a valid equation has matched units at every operator). Using a transformer NSR model (SymbolicGPT/DGSR-style) trained on the Feynman equations with per-variable units, plus sparse autoencoders on its residual stream, we (1) LOCATE candidate numerical-fit features and candidate dimensional-consistency features via probing; (2) CAUSALLY test the steerability of each, contrasting fit control against unit control; (3) INTERPRET whether located units encode a genuine dimensional-type concept or shallow token statistics; and (4) AUDIT reliability, testing whether an intervention-free dimensional-consistency signal flags silently-invalid equations better than fit or model likelihood. We predict fit is steerable, dimensional consistency is decodable-but-weakly-steerable, and a cheap internal audit catches dimensional violations before downstream physical use.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODEL (frozen): a transformer neural-symbolic-regression model, SymbolicGPT/DGSR-style, autoregressive over expression-tree tokens (~30-100M params), using a public checkpoint or one trained by us on the Feynman Symbolic Regression Database (100 physics equations, each with KNOWN SI units per variable) augmented with synthetic dimensioned datasets (assign SI units to variables, sample values, compute targets); ~8k train / 1k val / held-out equations for testing. The NSR model is FROZEN; only SAEs/probes are trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. DIMENSIONAL oracle (exact, deterministic, free): a unit-propagation checker that walks the generated expression tree, propagates each variable's SI dimension vector through operators (add/subtract require equal dimensions; multiply/divide add/subtract dimension vectors; log/exp/trig require a dimensionless argument; the whole equation must match the target dimension), returning a binary CONSISTENT flag and a graded VIOLATION SCORE (count/severity of mismatched operator nodes). FIT oracle: R^2 / normalized MSE of the generated equation against held-out data points. VALIDITY gate: parseable, well-formed expression tree. PRECONDITION: confirm the model natively produces a RANGE of both fit qualities AND dimensional-consistency states (consistent and inconsistent equations both occur), so absence-of-control claims are meaningful; also confirm variable units are ingested so the model COULD represent dimensions. Compute: one frozen NSR transformer + <=4 SAEs on a single GPU, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- numerical-fit features ARE causally steerable): Tests that fit-linked features exist and steer the generated equation's fit. Data: 2,000 held-out (data, equation) pairs, used as-is. Identify NUMERICAL-FIT features (probe AUROC / concept-correlation for "will fit well" on held-out partial equations, retain AUROC >= 0.7). For each of >=8 fit features, sweep steering strength (6 levels), generate 100 equations per level given fixed data, and measure the DECISIVE metric first: fit gain (Delta R^2) per unit steer, with specificity and a matched-norm random-direction control. Convincing: median fit gain per unit steer with Cohen's d >= 0.8 vs random control and monotone dose-response (Spearman |rho| >= 0.6) for a majority of features. Undecidable band: d in [0.2, 0.5) or |rho| in [0.2, 0.4) -> fit-steerability unestablished for that feature; drop it from H2's head-to-head. Negative result (d < 0.2 across features): fit itself is not steerable, the blind-spot premise collapses; reported as a controllability null.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- NO compact, causally-steerable dimensional-consistency handle): Tests that dimensional consistency is decodable-but-inert. (2a decodability) Probe SAE features and raw activations to predict the running dimension type of the partial expression / whether the next operator is dimensionally legal, using partial correlation to remove fit confounds; decisive metric: dimension-probe AUROC. (2b steerability) In the SAME pipeline as Experiment 1, attempt to lower the violation score / flip to CONSISTENT while HOLDING R^2 fixed, using four interventions (TopK SAE feature, Ordered/Matryoshka feature, difference-of-means between consistent/inconsistent completions, activation patching from consistent runs); decisive metric: dimensional-restoration success = fraction of steers that reduce the violation score to CONSISTENT while keeping |Delta R^2| within measurement noise. Convincing support for H2 (a real ABSENCE): dimension is decodable (2a AUROC >= 0.75) yet no intervention reaches > 0.2 restoration success and its effect size is < 1/3 of fit steerability (Experiment 1) -- decodable-but-inert. Undecidable band: 2a AUROC in [0.6, 0.7) (decodability itself unresolved -- report, do not claim inertness) OR restoration success in [0.2, 0.4) (a weak handle may exist -> claim "weak/partial", not absence). Negative result for H2 (restoration success >= 0.4 for any intervention, effect within 1/3 of fit): a genuine dimensional handle EXISTS -- an equally publishable positive enabling units-aware equation discovery; reported as refutation.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- fit-steering silently produces dimensionally invalid equations, invisible to R^2/likelihood): Tests the core blind spot. Reuse Experiment 1's fit-feature steers; at each strength measure the DECISIVE metric first: SILENT-INCONSISTENCY RATE = fraction of well-formed, better-fitting equations (Delta R^2 > 0) that are dimensionally INVALID; then blind-spot magnitude = increase in violation score per unit fit gain (dose-response); then INVISIBILITY = correlation between fit gain / model likelihood and true dimensional consistency. Random-direction and matched-non-fit-feature controls. Convincing: SILENT-INCONSISTENCY RATE >= 0.3 among better-fitting equations AND invisibility |r| <= 0.2 (better-fitting equations are no more dimensionally valid). Undecidable band: rate in [0.1, 0.3) or |r| in [0.2, 0.4) -> mild blind spot; report magnitude only. Negative result (rate < 0.1 or |r| > 0.4): fit-steering preserves dimensional consistency -- a valuable positive result that NSR feature-steering is dimensionally safe.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- an intervention-free internal dimensional-consistency signal flags and prunes invalid equations): Tests the audit payoff. Systems compared: internal dimensional-consistency score (dimension-probe confidence / feature coherence read mid-generation) vs output-side signals (fit, well-formedness, model likelihood) vs a black-box raw-activation probe. Labels from Experiment 3's oracle. Decisive metric first: detection AUROC for the fit-OK/units-broken class, then calibration ECE, then two operational payoffs -- search compute saved by pruning dimensionally-invalid candidates from the beam before full data-fitting, and improvement in TRUE-Feynman-equation recovery rate when the internal signal re-ranks/prunes the beam vs fit-only selection. Convincing: internal AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.1 above the best output-side signal, ECE <= 0.1, and dimensional re-ranking improves true-equation recovery by >= 5 percentage points over fit-only. Undecidable band: internal-minus-output-side AUROC gap in [0.0, 0.05] or recovery improvement in [1, 5) points -> marginal payoff; report without headline. Negative result (internal AUROC < 0.6 or recovery not improved): no usable internal dimensional signal; the audit payoff is withdrawn, leaving the blind-spot demonstration (Experiment 3) as the contribution.

Experiment 5 (interpretation + robustness of H2-H4): Test whether located dimensional units encode a genuine dimension-TYPE concept (invariant to specific variables/constants) vs shallow token/operator statistics, using controlled expression pairs that dissociate dimension from surface form (same structure, variables reassigned so consistency flips; different structure, identical dimension type); auto-label top features via max-activating contexts. Repeat Experiments 2-4 across two model sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, two layers, autoregressive vs diffusion (DiffuSR-style) NSR, and Feynman vs synthetic datasets; report the fraction of cells where the blind spot and non-steerability replicate and whether dimensional steerability is worse for equations needing transcendental-function dimensionlessness than pure polynomials. A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Dimensional consistency is an EXACT, non-proxy symbolic oracle (unit propagation is deterministic), which is a core strength; the main proxy is 'physical validity' beyond units, which we deliberately do not claim — claims concern the objectively-checkable dimensional invariant, not full physical correctness. 2) The dimensional-non-steerability claim is partly an ABSENCE claim; we mitigate by trying multiple intervention types (TopK/Ordered SAE features, difference-of-means, activation patching from consistent runs), sweeping strength, requiring the model to natively span a consistency range, and head-to-head calibrating that FIT features ARE steerable in the same pipeline — so a null dimensional result is meaningful, not a weak-model artifact. A positive result (a genuine steerable dimensional handle) is equally publishable and directly enables units-aware equation discovery without architectural surgery. 3) Fit and dimensional consistency are partly entangled (the true equation is both well-fitting and consistent); the partial-correlation feature selection and dimension-flipping dissociation pairs (step 5) isolate genuinely fit-independent dimensional signal, and we report where separation is impossible. 4) Some NSR checkpoints do not ingest units at all; we ensure the training data provides per-variable units (Feynman + synthetic) so the model COULD in principle represent dimensions, making the absence claim substantive. 5) SAE quality/layer choice could confound Location; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, raw-activation probes (which PATCHES shows are partly correlational, so we corroborate with causal patching), and random-direction controls. 6) An internal dimensional probe might not beat a black-box raw-activation probe on raw AUROC; the interpretability diagnosis (fit-steerable, dimensions-decodable-but-weakly-steerable, type-concept-vs-token-statistics) and the audit/search-pruning payoff remain the contributions, reported honestly. 7) If no blind spot is found (fit steering preserves dimensional consistency), that is a valuable positive result establishing that NSR feature-steering is dimensionally safe and that these models robustly represent physical units.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims are: (1) NSR transformers may encode numerical fit in steerable features; (2) they may lack a compact causal representation of dimensional consistency; (3) steering fit can silently generate dimensionally invalid equations; (4) an exact unit-propagation oracle can audit this blind spot; (5) this is a new interpretability target for symbolic/mathematical objects. Relative to PATCHES, the delta is real: from operator circuits in SR to a physically meaningful invariant and a fit-vs-units causal contrast. The main novelty is the mechanism/phenomenon in a new object class, not the model family itself. It is strong, but somewhat adjacent to existing units-aware SR work and interpretability-in-generated-sequences work.

Name: control_authority_vs_sampling_noise
Title: Signal or Seed Lottery? Whether Interpretable-Feature Steering Actually Controls Scientific Designs or Just Nudges a Distribution Swamped by Sampling Noise
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable-feature steering of scientific generative models is routinely reported as a mean property shift, but we hypothesize that for a large fraction of features the property VARIANCE induced by ordinary sampling stochasticity (seed/temperature) dwarfs the steering-induced mean shift, so a single steered generation is a seed lottery rather than deterministic control. We further hypothesize an intervention-free 'control-authority' score (steer-shift-to-sampling-spread ratio, estimable from a tiny sample) predicts which steers give reproducible per-object control versus which are effectively noise, and that this reframes when steering can be trusted for real one-shot design.
Related Work: All steering-of-generation work in science reports AGGREGATE mean property shifts: InterPLM (2024), ProtSAE (2025), Steering Protein Language Models/ASPO (2025), CB-pLM (2024), Automated Neuron Labelling (2025), Circuits/Features/Heuristics in Molecular Transformers (2025), Steering Vector Fields for Molecular Generation (2025), and Physics Steering (2025). Crucially, every one of these quantifies success as the average change in a target property across many generations and never separates the steering signal from the sampling-noise floor at the level of an individual design. Text-LLM work on steering-vector unreliability (Understanding the Unreliability of Steering Vectors 2026) studies cross-prompt/method fragility but not the signal-vs-sampling-noise decomposition, and not for scientific objects with objective oracles. The Steering-Vector-Fields paper even notes larger shifts come 'at the expense of validity' but never measures per-generation reproducibility. No prior work (a) decomposes steering-induced mean shift against the sampling-induced property variance to compute a per-feature control-authority ratio, (b) shows that many celebrated steers have authority near or below 1 (seed-lottery regime), or (c) provides a cheap predictor of which steers deliver reproducible one-shot control. This is distinct from my prior blind-spot proposals (which contrast property classes) by asking a stochasticity/reproducibility question about steering ITSELF.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design steers a feature and reports that the target property increased on average. But real design is often one-shot: you generate a design and use it. We ask whether a single steered generation actually delivers the intended property, or whether the property you get is dominated by which random seed you drew. Scientific generative models sample stochastically, so any target property already has a baseline VARIANCE across seeds and temperatures; steering adds a mean SHIFT. We hypothesize that for many interpretable features the shift is small relative to this sampling spread, placing steering in a seed-lottery regime where per-object control is illusory despite a real average effect. Using ESM-2 protein language models and a SMILES chemical language model with sparse autoencoders and exact/cheap property oracles (DSSP/ESMFold, GRAVY, molecular weight; RDKit logP, QED, ring counts), we (1) decompose, per feature, the steering-induced mean shift against the sampling-induced property variance to compute a Control-Authority ratio (Cohen's-d-style shift/spread); (2) establish the seed-lottery phenomenon by measuring the fraction of features whose authority is below a per-object-reliability threshold, and the resulting one-shot success rate; (3) test whether an intervention-free control-authority score estimated from a tiny sample predicts reproducible one-shot control better than the reported mean shift; and (4) show a practical fix—a small best-of-n selection budget guided by an internal property readout—that converts low-authority steers into reliable one-shot designs, tracing an authority-vs-selection-cost frontier. Results recast steering evaluation from mean shifts to per-design reliability.
Experiments:
Shared setup (fixed once, reused below). MODELS (frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (proteins); a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~85M, MOSES-trained or public checkpoint). Frozen; only SAEs/probes trainable. SAEs: TopK and Ordered/Matryoshka on the residual stream at an intrinsic-dimension-chosen layer (plus a second layer), width 16x, k=32, Adam lr 1e-3, ~40M activation tokens, seeds {0,1,2}; reconstruction accepted at fraction-variance-unexplained <=0.2. PROPERTY oracles (cheap/exact): proteins -- alpha-helix/beta-sheet content (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight; molecules -- logP, QED, ring/aromatic count (RDKit). VALIDITY gates: ESMFold pLDDT + pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity + SA (molecules). FEATURE BANK: ~30-50 interpretable property-linked features per domain (concept-correlation / probe AUROC) plus difference-of-means directions as a baseline. Compute: two ESM-2 sizes + small SMILES LM + ESMFold on 1-2 GPUs, academic-feasible.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- for many features the sampling-induced property variance dwarfs the steering-induced mean shift: a single steered draw is a seed lottery): Tests the core decomposition. For each feature/property at a fixed steering strength, generate 200 objects each UNSTEERED and STEERED across many seeds (plus a small temperature sweep). Decisive metric first: CONTROL-AUTHORITY ratio = steering mean shift / unsteered sampling std (a standardized effect size); then per-object OVERLAP = fraction of steered draws that do NOT clear the unsteered distribution's target-property threshold; then ONE-SHOT SUCCESS RATE = probability a single steered draw lands in the target band, contrasted with the AGGREGATE mean shift the steering literature would report (the "works on average vs works once" gap). Matched-norm random-direction control bounds spurious shift. Convincing (H1 holds): a LARGE fraction -- >= 0.3 of bank features -- have control-authority < 1.0 (mean shift below one sampling std) with one-shot success < 0.5, while their aggregate mean shift is nominally "successful", establishing the gap. Undecidable band: seed-lottery fraction in [0.15, 0.3) -> phenomenon present but limited; report the distribution, do not headline. Negative result (< 0.15 of features in the low-authority regime; most have authority >= 1.0 and one-shot success >= 0.5): steering gives reliable per-object control -- a valuable positive result that interpretable steering works one-shot, not just on average.

Experiment 2 (authority-vs-validity frontier -- ruling out that strength trivially buys authority): Supports H1 by showing the seed lottery is not an artifact of one weak strength. Sweep steering strength (6 levels) and, at each, recompute control-authority and validity. Decisive metric first: whether any strength reaches control-authority >= 1.0 at validity retained within 10% of unsteered, traced as an authority-vs-validity frontier. Convincing: for the low-authority features, higher strength raises authority only by driving validity down (no strength achieves authority >= 1.0 at acceptable validity). Undecidable band: a strength reaches authority in [0.8, 1.0) at acceptable validity -> borderline controllable; report the frontier. Negative result: a moderate strength achieves authority >= 1.0 at retained validity -- the seed-lottery framing is strength-specific, reported as such.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- a cheap, intervention-free control-authority score predicts which steers are reliable): Tests the predictor. Decisive metric first: Spearman rho / out-of-sample R^2 of full-sample control-authority (and one-shot success) predicted from a TINY sample (8-16 steered + 8-16 unsteered draws), then precision@k for flagging unreliable steers as a pre-flight check; also test an intervention-free GEOMETRIC predictor (decoder-direction norm relative to residual-stream norm; feature-decoder overlap) and compare both against the reported mean shift and concept-correlation (nested-model comparison). Convincing: the small-sample estimate predicts full-sample authority with |rho| >= 0.6 and precision@10 >= 0.7 for flagging seed-lottery steers, and the geometric predictor adds >= 0.1 R^2 over mean-shift/concept-correlation. Undecidable band: small-sample |rho| in [0.3, 0.5) or precision@10 in [0.5, 0.7) -> a noisy predictor; report the minimal sample size that reaches the band or that none does. Negative result (|rho| < 0.3): authority cannot be predicted cheaply -- the pre-flight-check contribution is withdrawn, leaving the phenomenon (Experiment 1) as the result.

Experiment 4 (payoff -- a selection budget converts seed-lottery steers into reliable control): Tests the practical fix. For low-authority steers apply best-of-n generation ranked by (a) a cheap internal property probe on the steered activation and (b) the external oracle; sweep n. Decisive metric first: one-shot (best-of-n) success rate vs n, traced as an authority-vs-selection-cost frontier -- how many extra samples convert a seed-lottery steer into reliable control, vs high-authority steers that need n=1; then compute cost of internal-probe vs oracle-guided selection. Convincing: best-of-n with internal-probe ranking reaches >= 0.8 success at n <= 8 for low-authority steers, within 2x the compute of oracle-guided selection. Undecidable band: required n in (8, 32] to reach 0.8 -> costly but usable; report the frontier. Negative result (success stays < 0.8 even at n=32, or internal-probe selection no better than random ranking): selection does not rescue low-authority steers cheaply -- reported honestly as a cost the seed lottery imposes.

Experiment 5 (robustness of H1-H2): Repeat across both domains, both ESM-2 sizes, TopK vs Ordered SAEs, difference-of-means baselines, and >=3 properties per domain, and test whether autoregressive generation shows lower authority (more accumulated noise) than masked-infilling. Report the fraction of cells where the seed-lottery regime and the authority predictor replicate, and the distribution of authority over reasonable target-band widths (the core claim uses the band-agnostic standardized ratio). A finding stable in <50% of cells is reported as regime-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles (ESMFold, DSSP, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal per-design controllability and reproducibility, not experimental function—stated explicitly, though property values are objective given the oracle. 2) Control-authority depends on the chosen target-property band width; we report authority as a distribution over reasonable bands and use a standardized effect-size that is band-agnostic for the core claim. 3) Higher steering strength could raise authority; we sweep strength fully and report the authority-vs-validity frontier so the seed-lottery finding is not an artifact of a single weak strength. 4) The small-sample authority predictor may be noisy; we quantify its calibration and the minimal sample size needed, and compare to intervention-free geometric predictors. 5) The best-of-n fix trades compute for reliability and depends on internal-probe quality; we report the frontier rather than claim a free lunch, and compare internal-probe vs oracle-guided selection. 6) SAE quality/layer choice could confound; controlled with TopK and Ordered SAEs, multiple layers, difference-of-means baselines, and random-direction controls. 7) If most steers turn out to have high authority (deterministic one-shot control), that is a valuable positive result establishing that interpretable-feature steering is reliable at the level of individual designs, not just on average.
